4.5 Construction results used in the proof

Building the profile takes three choices that have to work together. The outer flow fixes the pressure on the axis, the regular inner flow matches the outer flow’s five cumulative integrals, and the shear on the interval between them satisfies the admissible cone condition. Lemma 4.7 first solves the finite-dimensional moment problem. Lemma 4.8 and Proposition 4.10 then build the outer and inner flows, and Lemma 4.11 builds the periodic shear. These results provide the pieces used in the proof of Theorem 4.6. The appendices prove each construction in full at the references given below.

In these statements, a parameter derivative means a derivative with respect to η\eta, with every construction constant held fixed. For a function on [−1,1][-1,1], write ∥f∥Ck=max⁡0≤j≤ksup⁡η|∂ηjf|\|f\|_{C^k}=\max_{0\leq j\leq k}\sup_\eta|\partial_\eta^jf|. For vectors, use the largest component norm. Only finitely many of these norms have to be small when the parameters are chosen. After the parameters have been fixed, every other fixed derivative order has a finite bound.

Lemma 4.7.

Let α1,…,αm\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m be distinct real numbers. Let β1,…,βm\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m be nonnegative, nonzero smooth functions supported in ordered, disjoint compact intervals of (0,∞)(0,\infty). Then the matrix

Bij=∫0∞xαiβj(x)dxB_{ij}=\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha_i}\beta_j(x)\,dx is invertible. Its inverse and every fixed parameter derivative stay bounded for any smooth compact family that keeps these assumptions true.

There is also a more general statement. Let B(η)B(\eta) be a smooth invertible matrix on [−1,1][-1,1], let 𝒬η\mathcal Q_\eta be a smooth bilinear map, and let d∈C∞([−1,1];ℝm)d\in C^\infty([-1,1];\mathbb{R}^m). Fix an integer k≥0k\geq 0. Let νj\nu_j be the norm of multiplication by B−1B^{-1} on CjC^j, and let qjq_j be the bilinear norm of 𝒬\mathcal Q on CjC^j, for j=0,kj=0,k. If

8νj2qj∥d∥Cj≤1(j=0,k),8\nu_j^2q_j\|d\|_{C^j}\leq1\qquad(j=0,k), then the equation

B(η)c(η)+𝒬η(c(η),c(η))=d(η)B(\eta)c(\eta)+\mathcal Q_\eta(c(\eta),c(\eta))=d(\eta) has a smooth solution. It is the only solution with ∥c∥C0≤2ν0∥d∥C0\|c\|_{C^0}\leq 2\nu_0\|d\|_{C^0}, and it satisfies ∥c∥Ck≤2νk∥d∥Ck\|c\|_{C^k}\leq 2\nu_k\|d\|_{C^k}. When 𝒬=0\mathcal Q=0, no smallness condition is needed and the solution is c=B−1dc=B^{-1}d.

Proof.

These two claims are Lemmas A.1 and A.2. For the first, multilinearity gives

det⁡B=∫det⁡[xjαi]∏jβj(xj)dx1⋯dxm.\det B=\int\det[x_j^{\alpha_i}]\prod_j\beta_j(x_j)\,dx_1\cdots dx_m. When x1<⋯<xmx_1<\cdots<x_m, the determinant inside this integral has one fixed nonzero sign. To see why, any nonzero linear combination of mm distinct powers has at most m−1m-1 positive zeros, by induction and Rolle’s theorem. So the integral is nonzero.

For the second claim, on the ball of radius rj=2νj∥d∥Cjr_j=2\nu_j\|d\|_{C^j}, the iteration c↦B−1(d−𝒬(c,c))c\mapsto B^{-1}(d-\mathcal Q(c,c)) satisfies

∥B−1(d−𝒬(c,c))∥Cj≤rj/2+νjqjrj2≤rj,2νjqjrj≤12.\|B^{-1}(d-\mathcal Q(c,c))\|_{C^j}\leq r_j/2+\nu_jq_jr_j^2\leq r_j, \qquad 2\nu_jq_jr_j\leq\tfrac12. It is a contraction in C0C^0 and CkC^k. Starting the iteration from zero picks the same solution in both spaces. The pointwise implicit function theorem then shows that this solution is smooth. ◻

The exterior is built before the part near the axis. Requiring its pressure to vanish at infinity fixes the pressure value that the axis problem must use. The family below contains the heat-flow exterior and keeps several intervals available, so later changes can restore the required moments.

Proposition A.4 and Lemma A.5 provide the reference profiles and the common pressure value in part (i). The four intervals defined after (A.9) are the intervals in part (ii). The parameter MdM_d controls the decrease in the axial direction, TdT_d controls how long that decrease lasts in logarithmic radius, P*P_\ast is the initial azimuthal amplitude, and λ,h\lambda,h are the intermediate and outer exponents.

Lemma A.6 and Proposition A.7 replace the tail by the heat profile from part (iii). Once the other parameters have been fixed, those results keep the cone inequalities from part (iii) true for every sufficiently large XRX_R. ◻

The exterior is now prepared with the right moments and heat flow. Its stress was defined by integrating outward from the axis. To get the conclusions at the outer edge as well, it still needs a regular inner extension with the same moments. Once that condition is met, the stress can instead be integrated backward from infinity, and its limiting direction can be found explicitly.

These claims are Lemma A.8 and Proposition A.10. The four moment identities make the total residual integrals cancel. This gives the backward primitives shown above, which are the integrals from the current radius to infinity. The prepared terminal profile then gives the cone inequalities and (4.32). ◻

The missing inner extension can now be built. It must be smooth at the axis and must match the five cumulative integrals of the prepared exterior at a chosen joining radius. It uses the function Π0(η)\Pi_0(\eta) from Lemma 4.8 as its pressure value at X=0X=0.

The profiles now produce the leading field from Section 3, with its stress supported in the prescribed annulus. The next section corrects the higher-order residual terms found after (4.7).

5 Correcting the base flow to every order

Near the axis, the leading profiles (E,U,V0,Π)(E,U,V_0,\Pi) from Theorem 4.6 satisfy the balances in Equations (4.7) and (4.13). Axial viscosity and the remaining radial terms still appear in the residual, however. Add axisymmetric corrections to obtain the background (uB,pB)(u_B,p_B) described in Section 3 and Proposition 5.5. The velocity uBu_B is exactly divergence-free. Its momentum residual is the negative cylindrical divergence of the physical annular stress 𝒯phys\mathcal T_{\mathrm{phys}}, as in (5.41), plus an error ℰB\mathcal E_B that is bounded by every power of qq as q↓0q\downarrow 0. The same bounds hold for every fixed physical derivative on each compact range of profile coordinates. The annular stress becomes the input to the wave construction in Section 7.

These remaining terms appear at successive powers of q2hq^{2h} in Equations (5.3)–(5.6). At each order, Lemma 5.1 solves for a correction near the axis. Lemma 5.2 then extends that correction in the radial direction and imposes the five integral conditions that keep its stress supported in the prescribed annulus. The induction in Proposition 5.3 finishes the current order before using its coefficients to build the next one.

The leading profiles and all constants used to construct them stay fixed throughout. The resulting sequence of coefficients is the formal expansion (5.1); this does not assert that the unmodified infinite series converges. After this sequence is built, Lemma 5.4 produces smooth fields for q>0q>0 with the same asymptotic coefficients. The proof of Proposition 5.5 checks that this summation keeps incompressibility, the exterior velocity, and the required bounds on the residual.

5.1 Higher coefficients near the axis.

First solve the coefficient equations (5.2)–(5.6) near the axis, where the stress must remain zero. For n≥0n\ge 0, set λn=2nh\lambda_n=2nh, E0=EE_0=E, U0=UU_0=U, and Π0=Π\Pi_0=\Pi. Every coefficient profile is a function of (X,η)(X,\eta). Here the subscript zero now marks the order in the expansion. The linear equations must be solvable on the same radial interval at every order. For that to work, the recursion needs bounds on its η\eta-derivatives even as the coefficient bounds grow. The analytic dependence of the leading inner profile gives those bounds.

Lemma 5.1.

There is an interval 0≤ξ≤a0\le\xi\le a, where ξ=X\xi=\sqrt X, that starts at the axis and extends into the inner collar from Theorem 4.6(i). The stress cone inequalities hold there with one uniform positive margin. On this interval, every positive order has exactly one solution of Equations (5.2)–(5.6) with ϕn(0,η)=Un(0,η)=Πn(0,η)=0\phi_n(0,\eta)=U_n(0,\eta)=\Pi_n(0,\eta)=0. The profiles are smooth in XX. For each fixed radial derivative, they are holomorphic on a neighborhood of [−1,1][-1,1] in the parameter η\eta, which means that they have a complex derivative at every point of that neighborhood. The neighborhood and its bounds may depend on the order and the radial derivative, but aa does not. The uniqueness statement applies among solutions whose profiles extend holomorphically in η\eta to a neighborhood of [−1,1][-1,1], with bounds uniform for 0≤ξ≤a0\le\xi\le a.

Because every positive-order coefficient is zero at the axis, the leading traces of ϕ,U, and Π\phi,U,\text{ and }\Pi stay unchanged.

5.3 The coefficient induction and the residual left by a finite sum

The last two lemmas build and extend one coefficient after all lower orders have been finished. Lemma 5.1 solves the inner equations (5.2) through (5.6). Lemma 5.2 extends that solution and gives its support properties while keeping those equations unchanged on 0≤X≤X−0\leq X\leq X_-. This subsection applies the two lemmas repeatedly and estimates the residual left by every finite truncation in (5.25), including its physical derivatives. The gain in decay must rise with the truncation order, while the loss in the exponent caused by physical differentiation must not depend on that order. Equation (5.26) gives the exact bound.

For a tuple VV of physical fields, write |V|m=max|α|+b≤m|∂xα∂tbV|.\begin{equation} |V|_m=\max_{|\alpha|+b\leq m}|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^bV|. \tag{5.23} \end{equation}(5.23) At the point in question, this is the largest absolute value among all Cartesian space–time derivatives of the tuple through order mm. Write un=ur,ner+uθ,neθ+uz,nezu_n=u_{r,n}e_r+u_{\theta,n}e_\theta+u_{z,n}e_z for the physical velocity coefficient in (5.1), and write 𝒯0\mathcal T_0 for the leading stress profile from (4.11).

Before putting any cutoff in qq, define the finite tuple 𝒰[N]=(uslow[N],pslow[N],Tslow[N])=∑n=0N(un,pn,q−A−1/2+λn𝒯n).\mathcal U^{[N]}= (u_{\mathrm{slow}}^{[N]},p_{\mathrm{slow}}^{[N]},T_{\mathrm{slow}}^{[N]}) =\sum_{n=0}^{N}(u_n,p_n,q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n}\mathcal T_n). The profiles in this sum already contain their radial cutoffs and moment corrections. For a physical stress pair T=(Tθ,Tz)T=(T_\theta,T_z), define ℱslow(u,p,T)=ℛ(u,p)+(∂r+2/r)Tθeθ+(∂r+1/r)Tzez.\begin{equation} \mathcal F_{\mathrm{slow}}(u,p,T)=\mathscr R(u,p) +(\partial_r+2/r)T_\theta e_\theta+(\partial_r+1/r)T_ze_z. \tag{5.24} \end{equation}(5.24) The last two terms are the tangential divergence of the stress that is being kept for the later wave construction.

Proposition 5.3.

Fix the leading profiles from Theorem 4.6. There is a sequence of positive-order profiles, with each order built first by Lemma 5.1 and then by Lemma 5.2 after all lower orders have been finalized. Every finite velocity sum uslow[N]u_{\mathrm{slow}}^{[N]} is divergence-free. Take any fixed compact profile range 0≤X≤Xmax0\leq X\leq X_{\max}, −1≤η≤1-1\leq\eta\leq 1, with 0<Xmax<∞0<X_{\max}<\infty. For every N,m≥0N,m\geq 0 and 0<q≤10<q\leq 1, the augmented momentum residual obeys |ℱslow(𝒰[N])|m≤CN,mq2h(N+1)−Km,Kmindependent of N.\begin{equation} |\mathcal F_{\mathrm{slow}}(\mathcal U^{[N]})|_m \leq C_{N,m}q^{2h(N+1)-K_m}, \qquad K_m\ \text{independent of }N. \tag{5.25} \end{equation}(5.25) The constants can depend on the fixed profile range. The constant CN,mC_{N,m} can depend on NN, while the loss KmK_m in the exponent does not.

Proof.

Step 1. Build the sequence and cancel every coefficient that has been kept. At order nn, apply Lemma 5.1 with the finalized orders 0,…,n−10,\ldots,n-1. Next apply Lemma 5.2. This extends and corrects the current profiles, rebuilds Vn,ΠnV_n,\Pi_n from Equations (5.2) and (5.5), and defines 𝒯n\mathcal T_n by (5.9). These operations keep the equations unchanged on the inner interval that was retained, and they keep the regularity needed to form Ωn/X\Omega_n/X at the next order. Both lemmas use the same fixed radial intervals, so this process continues for every nn.

Equation (5.2) gives exact incompressibility at each order, and hence for every finite sum. The pressure equation holds everywhere. Differentiating the stress primitives gives (∂R+2/R)𝒯n,θ=−𝔯θ,n,(∂R+1/R)𝒯n,z=−𝔯z,n.(\partial_R+2/R)\mathcal T_{n,\theta}=-\mathfrak r_{\theta,n}, \qquad (\partial_R+1/R)\mathcal T_{n,z}=-\mathfrak r_{z,n}. Thus the tangential residual at each retained order is exactly the negative of the stress divergence. Proposition 4.2 gives the same leading identities at order zero. Once the sum has been cut off at NN, every product or shifted viscosity term that has not been canceled has an exponent increment of at least 2h(N+1)2h(N+1). For example, when N=1N=1, both the product of two order-one velocity coefficients and axial viscosity applied to order one first appear at order two.

Step 2. Estimate the physical derivatives of the finite residual. The coordinate formulas show exactly how physical differentiation changes the powers of qq. Suppose that g(x⟂/q,η)g(x_\perp/\sqrt q,\eta) is smooth in its Cartesian arguments on a compact profile range. If there are a=|β|a=|\beta| transverse derivatives, kk axial derivatives, and ll time derivatives, then |∂x⟂β∂zk∂tl[qbg(x⟂/q,η)]|≤Cm(1+|b|)m∥g∥Cmqb−a/2−Dk−l,m=a+k+l.\begin{equation} \left|\partial_{x_\perp}^{\beta}\partial_z^k\partial_t^l \bigl[q^b g(x_\perp/\sqrt q,\eta)\bigr]\right| \leq C_m(1+|b|)^m\|g\|_{C^m}q^{b-a/2-Dk-l}, \qquad m=a+k+l. \tag{5.26} \end{equation}(5.26)

This follows from the chain rule and the identities ∂t=q−1L−1(−q∂q+X∂X+Dη∂η)\partial_t=q^{-1}L^{-1}(-q\partial_q+X\partial_X+D\eta\partial_\eta) and ∂z=q−DL−1(2ηq∂q−2ηX∂X+d∂η)\partial_z=q^{-D}L^{-1}(2\eta q\partial_q-2\eta X\partial_X+d\partial_\eta). Each transverse derivative of these smooth Cartesian profiles contributes a factor q−1/2q^{-1/2}.

The powers of nn produced by differentiating qλnq^{\lambda_n} are absorbed into the coefficient constants. The reduction in the exponent depends only on how many physical derivatives of each kind are taken. On the common stress support, X≥Xa>0X\geq X_a>0, so r−1=q−1/2(2X)−1/2r^{-1}=q^{-1/2}(2X)^{-1/2} also has derivative losses that do not depend on NN. Near the axis, use the smooth Cartesian representative of the velocity instead. A fixed truncated residual contains only finitely many terms. Applying (5.26) to those terms proves (5.25), with KmK_m independent of NN. ◻

5.4 Adding the coefficients while keeping zero divergence

The finite tuples 𝒰[N]\mathcal U^{[N]} have residuals with better and better decay in (5.25), but the constants Cn,mC_{n,m} in the coefficient bounds (5.17) can grow too quickly for the entire formal series (5.1) to converge. To obtain smooth fields, multiply the nn th positive-order term by χ(cnq)\chi(c_nq). Here χ=1\chi=1 near zero and χ=0\chi=0 once its argument reaches one, and the constants are chosen with cn→∞c_n\to\infty, as in (5.34). To keep the velocity incompressible, apply the cutoffs to vector potentials before differentiating them. An axisymmetric Stokes streamfunction SS gives such a potential. If S/r2S/r^2 is smooth as a function of (r2,z,t)(r^2,z,t), then 𝒜=Sreθ=Sr2(−x2,x1,0),curl⁡𝒜=−∂zSrer+∂rSrez.\mathcal A=\frac Sr e_\theta=\frac S{r^2}(-x_2,x_1,0), \qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathcal A=-\frac{\partial_zS}{r}e_r+\frac{\partial_rS}{r}e_z. In fact, curl⁡𝒜n=ur,ner+uz,nez\operatorname{curl}\mathcal A_n=u_{r,n}e_r+u_{z,n}e_z, so the curl gives exactly the radial and axial velocity components. In Cartesian coordinates, r2=2qXr^2=2qX gives 𝒜n=𝒮nr2(−x2,x1,0)=12q−A+λnFnX(−x2,x1,0).\mathcal A_n=\frac{\mathcal S_n}{r^2}(-x_2,x_1,0) =\frac12q^{-A+\lambda_n}\frac{F_n}{X}(-x_2,x_1,0). Cutting off 𝒜n\mathcal A_n and then taking its curl includes the extra velocity term that comes from differentiating the cutoff, so the result remains divergence-free. The summation argument will be stated for tuples of physical fields, which also allows it to be used later for the wave and mean correction sequence. In the present case, the index j=nj=n, the decay order is gn=2nhg_n=2nh, and the entries are An=𝒜n,Bn=uθ,neθ,pn=q−2A+λnΠn,Tn=q−A−1/2+λn𝒯n.A_n=\mathcal A_n, \qquad B_n=u_{\theta,n}e_\theta, \qquad p_n=q^{-2A+\lambda_n}\Pi_n, \qquad T_n=q^{-A-1/2+\lambda_n}\mathcal T_n. The differential polynomial is ℱslow\mathcal F_{\mathrm{slow}} from (5.24). Inside the lemma, UjU_j names a tuple of physical fields, not the axial profile Un(X,η)U_n(X,\eta). Use the derivative notation in (5.23), and set Λlog(q)=1+|log⁡q|\Lambda_{\log}(q)=1+|\log q|. Every estimate in the lemma is uniform on the domain stated there.

The general argument needs one common domain, decay orders that rise to infinity, and derivative losses that do not depend on the summation index. First bound the derivatives of every cutoff. Then choose the cutoffs so that the tail remains summable after any fixed number of derivatives, and compare the residual with one finite partial sum before the cutoffs are applied. 6 The auxiliary torus and the separation of oscillatory supports

Fix the background velocity uBu_B, the pressure pBp_B, and the annular stress 𝒯phys\mathcal T_{\mathrm{phys}} from Proposition 5.5. The momentum residual is the divergence of that stress, with the sign used in (5.41), plus a flat remainder. The waves in Proposition 7.5 will supply the leading stress. Their amplitudes change under the local shear of the background according to (7.5). Before those waves can be built, they must be confined to regions where the local estimates control the variation of the shear. Their supports must also be arranged so that different waves do not create extra quadratic interactions. At the same time, this localization must allow rapid changes in time without creating radial derivatives large enough to ruin the residual estimates.

Introduce the periodic variable Y∈𝕋2=ℝ2/ℤ2Y\in\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2, independently of the physical coordinates (r,θ,z,t)(r,\theta,z,t). Physical fields are then obtained by evaluating it at the fixed map depending on (r,t)(r,t) in (6.3). This map lets time vary rapidly while adding much smaller radial derivatives. The time variation drives the pulse equation in Section 7, and the bounds on the radial derivatives control the errors caused by localization. Oscillations whose supports overlap in the remaining variables are given disjoint auxiliary supports, so their cross products vanish after evaluation. Different harmonics of the same localized oscillation still interact.

First, derive the evaluated derivative operators in (6.6). Lemma 6.1 separates the supports, and Lemma 6.2 puts overlapping bands into one common representation. Section 6.4 then defines the coefficient classes, and Proposition 6.6 gives their rules for products and derivatives.

Every preliminary geometric choice is made on the one domain 0<q<qbig0<q<q_{\mathrm{big}}. The number qbigq_{\mathrm{big}} may be made smaller when the fixed base and pulse coefficients are chosen, before the correction iteration starts.

Lemma 6.1.

For the labels Γ\Gamma and slow supports KγK_\gamma in Equations (6.8) and (6.9), there are centers cγc_\gamma and one radius r0>0r_0>0, shared by every label and independent of the band, with two properties. First, the enlarged rectangles in (6.10) are parametrized injectively. Second,

γ≠γ′,Kγ∩Kγ′≠⌀⇒ℛγabs,+¯∩ℛγ′abs,+¯=⌀.\begin{equation} \gamma\ne\gamma',\qquad K_\gamma\cap K_{\gamma'}\ne\varnothing \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \overline{\mathcal R_\gamma^{\mathrm{abs},+}} \cap \overline{\mathcal R_{\gamma'}^{\mathrm{abs},+}} =\varnothing. \tag{6.13} \end{equation}(6.13)

Proof.

Step 1: bound how many interactions are possible. If two dyadic supports meet, then q/Q,q/Q′∈[1/2,2]q/Q,q/Q'\in[1/2,2], so |ℓ−ℓ′|≤2|\ell-\ell'|\le 2. Enlarge every mesh box by one fixed factor. Join two different labels when their enlarged slow boxes meet in physical coordinates and their band indices differ by at most four. Also join the two opposite signs of the same box. The resulting graph has

bounded degree. In fact, when |ℓ−ℓ′|≤4|\ell-\ell'|\le 4, the change of physical scale in each coordinate is bounded, and so is the ratio ℓ2/(ℓ′)2\ell^2/(\ell')^2. A box can then meet only a bounded number of enlarged boxes in any of those bands. Neither the degrees nor the number of colors needed depends on the band.

The differences between the covering indices i(ℓ)i(\ell) also have one fixed bound. If every band has ℓ≥ℓ0\ell\ge\ell_0, then |ℓ−ℓ′|≤4|\ell-\ell'|\le 4 gives

|i(ℓ)−i(ℓ′)|≤1+4(1+h)log⁡2+8/ℓ0log⁡Tg≤Δmax,\begin{equation} |i(\ell)-i(\ell')| \le 1+\frac{4(1+h)\log2+8/\ell_0}{\log T_g} \le\Delta_{\max}, \tag{6.14} \end{equation}(6.14) after choosing an integer upper bound. To get this estimate, subtract ((1+h)ℓlog⁡2−2log⁡ℓ)/log⁡Tg((1+h)\ell\log 2-2\log\ell)/\log T_g at the two band indices and use the mean value theorem. Taking the floor adds at most one.

Step 2: separate the centers under the coverings that matter. Color the countable graph greedily, using only finitely many colors. Choose one rational center cν∈𝕋2c_\nu\in\mathbb T^2 for each color ν\nu, and set cγ=cνc_\gamma=c_\nu whenever γ\gamma has that color. Choose the color centers so that all the following ordered constraints hold.

cμ≠JgΔcν(mod⁡ℤ2)(0≤Δ≤Δmax),unless (Δ,ν,μ)=(0,ν,ν).\begin{equation} c_\mu\ne J_g^\Delta c_\nu\pmod{\mathbb Z^2} \quad (0\le\Delta\le\Delta_{\max}), \qquad \text{unless }(\Delta,\nu,\mu)=(0,\nu,\nu). \tag{6.15} \end{equation}(6.15) Every excluded equality is a proper closed condition on the finite tuple of centers. When the two colors are the same and Δ>0\Delta>0, this follows because JgΔ−IJ_g^\Delta-I is invertible. The complement of all these conditions is open and dense, and it contains a rational tuple. This leaves every one of the finitely many forbidden differences a positive distance from the integer lattice.

Step 3: choose one size for every rectangle. Take rectangles in the eigenvector coordinates around these centers. Make them small enough both to be injective on the band torus and to keep the separation after the fixed enlargement. If a point belonged to the lifted rectangles of two adjacent labels at levels ii and i+Δi+\Delta, it would give cμ−JgΔcν=JgΔeν−eμc_\mu-J_g^\Delta c_\nu=J_g^\Delta e_\nu-e_\mu modulo the lattice, with |eν|+|eμ|≤Cr0|e_\nu|+|e_\mu|\le Cr_0. Since Δ\Delta has a fixed finite bound, one fixed r0r_0 small enough makes this contradict (6.15). Step 1 joined every pair whose slow supports overlap. This proves (6.13), including the separation needed for the supports of derivatives. ◻

For the rest of the construction, fix the centers cγc_\gamma and the radius r0r_0 from Lemma 6.1, along with one integer Δmax\Delta_{\max} that satisfies (6.14). In particular, take a family (Fγ)γ∈Γ(F_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma} whose supports in (r,z,t,Y)(r,z,t,Y) are uniform in θ\theta. Then

[supp⁡Fγ⊂Kγ×ℛγabs,+ for all γ∈Γ]⇒FγFγ′=0(γ≠γ′).\bigl[\operatorname{supp}F_\gamma\subset K_\gamma\times\mathcal R_\gamma^{\mathrm{abs},+} \text{ for all }\gamma\in\Gamma\bigr] \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F_\gamma F_{\gamma'}=0 \quad(\gamma\ne\gamma'). The same identity holds for derivatives of smoothly extended fields, and it still holds after evaluation on (6.3).

Choose a nonzero smooth transverse cutoff χg∈Cc∞((−r0,r0))\chi_g\in C_c^\infty((-r_0,r_0)), with 0≤χg≤10\le\chi_g\le 1. Rescale one fixed function to get the time cutoff 0≤ψ≤10\le\psi\le 1, with

ψ(v)=1if |v−Ls/2|≤Ls/5,supp⁡ψ⊂{|v−Ls/2|<Ls/3}.\begin{equation} \psi(v)=1\quad\text{if }|v-L_s/2|\le L_s/5, \qquad \operatorname{supp}\psi\subset\{|v-L_s/2|<L_s/3\}. \tag{6.16} \end{equation}(6.16) These cutoffs stay strictly inside the enlarged rectangles. Once the pulse equation has been solved there, multiplication by ψ\psi keeps its time support inside the rectangle.

6.3 One common torus for overlapping bands

The rectangle ℛγ\mathcal R_\gamma from (6.10), for a label in band ℓ\ell, is written in the band coordinate Yi=πi(ℓ)(Y)Y_i=\pi_{i(\ell)}(Y) from (6.5). for this change of representation and keeps normalized Haar averages unchanged. Fix (z,t)(z,t) with 0<q(z,t)<qbig0<q(z,t)<q_{\mathrm{big}}. In a small enough neighborhood UU of this point, set

∑ℓ∈ℒ(U)fℓ(Yi(ℓ))=∑ℓ∈ℒ(U)fℓ(JgΔℓH).\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L(U)}f_\ell(Y_{i(\ell)}) =\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L(U)}f_\ell(J_g^{\Delta_\ell}H).

Lemma 6.2.

Take U,i0,HU,i_0,H as in (6.17). Every change H↦YiH\mapsto Y_i has derivative factors bounded by one constant that works for every band. The set ℛγH\mathcal R_\gamma^H is made of 14Δℓ≤14Δmax14^{\Delta_\ell}\le 14^{\Delta_{\max}} disjoint lifts of ℛγ\mathcal R_\gamma. Whenever a function is pulled back from the torus in question, its Haar average is the same on the absolute, common, and band tori. Proof.

Step 1: compare the covering maps and their averages. Write Δ=Δℓ\Delta=\Delta_\ell. The matrix norms of JgΔJ_g^\Delta are bounded because 0≤Δ≤Δmax0\le\Delta\le\Delta_{\max}. The preimage rectangles are indexed by the finite quotient below.

ℛγH=⨆[k]∈ℤ2/JgΔℤ2{Jg−Δ(cγ+k+ξvr+ηvt)(mod⁡ℤ2):|ξ|,|η|<r0},#(ℤ2/JgΔℤ2)=|det⁡Jg|Δ=14Δ.\begin{aligned} \mathcal R_\gamma^H &=\bigsqcup_{[k]\in\mathbb Z^2/J_g^\Delta\mathbb Z^2} \bigl\{J_g^{-\Delta}(c_\gamma+k+\xi v_r+\eta v_t) \pmod{\mathbb Z^2}:|\xi|,|\eta|<r_0\bigr\},\\ \#(\mathbb Z^2/J_g^\Delta\mathbb Z^2) &=|\det J_g|^\Delta=14^\Delta. \end{aligned} Here cγc_\gamma is the representative already chosen in ℝ2\mathbb R^2. ∫𝕋2f(JgΔH)dH=∫𝕋2f(Yi)dYi.\begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb T^2} f(J_g^\Delta H)\,dH =\int_{\mathbb T^2} f(Y_i)\,dY_i. \tag{6.19} \end{equation}(6.19) A character with frequency nn pulls back to one with frequency (JgΔ)Tn(J_g^\Delta)^Tn. This new frequency is zero exactly when n=0n=0, which proves the equality.

Step 2: keep the common representation under all the stated operations. Radial integration fixes (z,t)(z,t), so it also fixes q=q(z,t)q=q(z,t). It leaves every band cutoff unchanged, even if the integral passes through many radial grid boxes. Translations on the torus commute with deck translations. Averaging and directional Fourier multipliers keep the lattice of pullback frequencies unchanged. This proves every preservation claim in the lemma. ◻

Fields are defined on the extended domain, where YY is independent, and use the original physical normalization. The common torus only gives a local way to represent them. fU(R,Z,T,Jgi0(U)Y)=fV(R,Z,T,Jgi0(V)Y)\begin{equation} f_U(R,Z,T,J_g^{i_0(U)}Y)=f_V(R,Z,T,J_g^{i_0(V)}Y) \tag{6.20} \end{equation}(6.20) at every point over U∩VU\cap V. Radial integration may collect more terms than pointwise multiplication. The next lemma counts the sums over slow labels that can appear. When several bands are compared, write Sℓ=ℓ2S_\ell=\ell^2.

Lemma 6.3 (Number of relevant labels).

There is a constant CC, independent of the band and the point, such that

sup(r,z,t)#{γ∈Γ:(r,z,t)∈Kγ}≤C.\sup_{(r,z,t)}\#\{\gamma\in\Gamma:(r,z,t)\in K_\gamma\}\le C. Fix a band ℓ\ell, a compact chart set B⊂ℝ3B\subset\mathbb R^3, and a bounded normalized radial interval IRI_R. Then

#{(ℓ,a,σ)∈Γ:Bℓ,a∩B≠⌀}≤CBSℓ9,supZ,T#{(ℓ,a,σ)∈Γ:Bℓ,a∩(IR×{Z}×{T})≠⌀}≤CIRSℓ3.\begin{aligned} \#\{(\ell,a,\sigma)\in\Gamma:B_{\ell,a}\cap B\ne\varnothing\} &\le C_BS_\ell^9,\\ \sup_{Z,T}\#\{(\ell,a,\sigma)\in\Gamma: B_{\ell,a}\cap(I_R\times\{Z\}\times\{T\})\ne\varnothing\} &\le C_{I_R}S_\ell^3. \end{aligned} The same bounds hold after enlarging the mesh boxes by any fixed factor.

At one point, the dyadic partition and every one-dimensional grid partition have bounded overlap. The two signs contribute a factor of two. On a bounded interval, a mesh of size Sℓ−3S_\ell^{-3} has O(Sℓ3)O(S_\ell^3) positions. A compact chart lets all three coordinates vary, so it contains O(Sℓ9)O(S_\ell^9) boxes. A radial line lets only one coordinate vary, so it meets O(Sℓ3)O(S_\ell^3) boxes. Enlarging the boxes by a fixed factor changes only the constants. ◻

The possible bands stay fixed during radial integration.

ℒ(z,t)={ℓ:(z,t)∈𝒟ℓ},q=q(z,t) is independent of r.\mathcal L(z,t)=\{\ell:(z,t)\in \mathcal D_\ell\}, \qquad q=q(z,t)\text{ is independent of }r. All these SℓS_\ell are comparable. Counting the lifts on the common torus adds at most the fixed factor 14Δmax14^{\Delta_{\max}}. To solve an amplitude equation from the beginning of a pulse up to its current coordinate vv, use the earlier points on that same lifted rectangle. The slow and transverse coordinates stay fixed along this path. A source built from several bands may be a function of HH without being a function of one particular YiY_i, because it may take different values at the different preimages of that point on the band torus. For this reason, describe the path separately on every lifted rectangle. The linear functional λt(w)=vt⋅w/(1+bg2)\lambda_t(w)=v_t\cdot w/(1+b_g^2) satisfies λt(vr)=0\lambda_t(v_r)=0 and λt(vt)=1\lambda_t(v_t)=1. Inside one lifted band rectangle, write ηg(H)=λt(JgΔH−cγ−kcopy)\eta_g(H)=\lambda_t(J_g^\Delta H-c_\gamma-k_{\mathrm{copy}}). For w∈[0,Ls]w\in[0,L_s], define

Hw=H+Tg−Δci(w−v(H))vt=H0+Tg−Δciwvt,H0=H−Tg−Δ(ηg(H)+r0)vt.\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} H_w&=H+T_g^{-\Delta}c_i\bigl(w-v(H)\bigr)v_t\\ &=H_0+T_g^{-\Delta}c_iwv_t, & H_0&=H-T_g^{-\Delta}\bigl(\eta_g(H)+r_0\bigr)v_t. \end{aligned} \tag{6.21} \end{equation}(6.21) This point has the same slow coordinates and the same band transverse coordinate ξg\xi_g, while its pulse coordinate is ww. Along this path, a source f(R,Z,T,H)f(R,Z,T,H) is evaluated as f(R,Z,T,Hw)f(R,Z,T,H_w). The other preimages are not averaged together. Since λtJgΔ=TgΔλt\lambda_tJ_g^\Delta=T_g^\Delta\lambda_t, fixing ww gives

DHHw=I−vtλt,DHv=TgΔciλt=O(S*).\begin{equation} D_HH_w=I-v_t\lambda_t, \qquad D_Hv=\frac{T_g^\Delta}{c_i}\lambda_t=O(S_*). \tag{6.22} \end{equation}(6.22)

Every higher derivative of these affine maps is zero. In the original auxiliary coordinate YY, the same path is Y′=Y+Tg−i(ηg′−ηg)vtY'=Y+T_g^{-i}(\eta_g'-\eta_g)v_t. A deck translation that keeps HH unchanged translates this path by the same amount and relabels the copy of the rectangle. It follows that the unique solution with zero initial data descends to the common torus. Proposition 7.2 proves the exact differentiated inverse estimate. Equation (6.22) supplies the needed coordinate change without adding another power of ε\varepsilon.

6.4 Coefficient bounds and their algebra

The residual estimates have to track both the size of a correction and the way it vanishes at the edge of its support. Let f,gf,g stand for angular mean coefficients, and let a,ba,b stand for labelled wave amplitudes. Their products and normalized derivatives occur in the correction equations, for example

fg,fa,ab,Drf,Dra.fg,\qquad fa,\qquad ab,\qquad D_rf,\qquad D_ra. Definitions 6.4 and 6.5 introduce three classes. They record the size of a mean coefficient, the size of a wave amplitude, and the size of a radial moment, in that order.

f∈𝖬α,aγ,m∈𝖶α,F(Z,T)∈𝖲α.f\in\mathsf M_\alpha, \qquad a_{\gamma,m}\in\mathsf W_\alpha, \qquad F(Z,T)\in\mathsf S_\alpha. The exponent α\alpha records a power of ε\varepsilon. The weight ζ\zeta in (6.23) measures how the function vanishes in the radial direction. An envelope PvP_v measures its decay in time and satisfies 0<Pv≤10<P_v\le 1 when 0≤v≤Ls0\le v\le L_s. Equation (7.12) will give the formula for this envelope. The estimates are required at every fixed derivative order. This makes the extensions across the shell smooth and keeps the bounds valid under the products and derivatives in Proposition 6.6.

Recall the flat edge weight from Theorem 4.6. On the fixed active interval Xa<X<XbX_a<X<X_b, it can be written as

ζ(X)=exp⁡(−aalog⁡2(X/Xa)−ablog⁡2(Xb/X)),δ(X)=min⁡{1,log⁡(X/Xa),log⁡(Xb/X)},\begin{equation} \zeta(X)=\exp\!\left( -\frac{a_a}{\log^2(X/X_a)}-\frac{a_b}{\log^2(X_b/X)} \right), \qquad \delta(X)=\min\{1,\log(X/X_a),\log(X_b/X)\}, \tag{6.23} \end{equation}(6.23) where aa,ab>0a_a,a_b>0 are fixed. Extend ζ\zeta by zero outside the interval. For every b>0b>0 and every finite NN, the quantity ζbδ−N\zeta^b\delta^{-N} goes to zero faster than every power at either endpoint. Both ζ\zeta and δ\delta depend only on XX, so they remain constant along the path in (6.21).

The phase varies rapidly, but its amplitude has a different derivative scale. A coefficient derivative differentiates only the amplitude after the oscillatory exponential has been factored out. Fix a finite stage jj and use normalized chart representatives. For a coefficient aa, write

∂Ia=∂RI1∂ZI2∂TI3∂H1I4∂H2I5a,I∈ℕ05.\partial^Ia =\partial_R^{I_1}\partial_Z^{I_2}\partial_T^{I_3} \partial_{H_1}^{I_4}\partial_{H_2}^{I_5}a, \qquad I\in\mathbb N_0^5. The derivatives in the auxiliary coordinates measure each representative separately, and the chain rule transforms them when i0i_0 changes. In the definitions below, Cj,I>0C_{j,I}>0 and bj,I,dj,I≥0b_{j,I},d_{j,I}\ge 0 may depend on j,Ij,I and the fixed profile data. They are uniform in the band, label, rectangle copy, and point.

7 Building the oscillations and correcting the residual stress

Fix the background (uB,pB)(u_B,p_B) from Proposition 5.5, along with the charts, slow cutoffs, and auxiliary rectangles from Equations (6.1), (6.9), and (6.10). The next step is to build waves whose averaged quadratic velocity products give the prescribed radial fluxes of azimuthal and axial momentum in the leading stress 𝒯0\mathcal T_0, with the physical normalization in (7.30). Their principal linearized evolution also has to match the background shear and viscous diffusion in (7.5). The supports make it possible to solve these problems locally and add the waves without cross terms between different labels, by Lemma 6.1. Later corrections use the same amplitude equation with a prescribed harmonic source, solved with the inverse from Proposition 7.2. A second linear operator, ℒ\mathcal L from Proposition 7.6, prescribes a signed change in the leading covariance.

The same linear amplitude equation, set by the background shear and viscosity, lies behind each part of the construction. Choose phases for which the homogeneous solution tσht^{\mathrm h}_{\sigma} in Lemma 7.4 first grows and then decays. Its Gaussian bound (7.16) makes it exponentially small near both ends of its interval. This solution is called a pulse. Compute the covariance, meaning the averaged quadratic velocity product, of two pulses with different phase gradients, and choose their amplitudes so that this covariance matches the stress. The strict cone condition (7.1) makes the squared amplitudes positive in Proposition 7.5. Once those positive amplitudes are fixed, linearizing there allows later stress increments with either sign. Finally, take curls of supported vector potentials so that the velocity is exactly incompressible, as Lemma 7.7 does. The extra velocity terms and the cutoff errors remain in the covariance estimate in Corollary 7.8 and in the residual identity (7.40).

Every calculation uses normalized representatives in the charts until the physical factors are shown. Before taking any derivative, fix the band, its representative, its discrete labels, and its integer frequencies. Constants for derivatives of any fixed order may depend on the fixed profiles and on that order. In applications, they may also depend on the finite correction stage. They stay uniform across the bands, labels, and copies of the rectangles.

7.2 Solving the pulse equation and controlling its derivatives

The frame BB from Lemma 7.1 turns (7.5) into an ordinary differential equation along each pulse. First solve it with zero initial amplitude and a prescribed source fmf_m. This gives the linear inverse used in Proposition 7.2 to remove later harmonics. Then solve the equation with zero source and a specified nonzero initial amplitude. That solution produces the pulses used for the leading covariance in Lemma 7.4. Both solutions must decay at both ends of the interval before they can be localized. P(v)=exp⁡(∫Ls/2v(λ(w)−dref(w))dw).\begin{equation} P(v)=\exp\left(\int_{L_s/2}^{v}(\lambda(w)-d_{\mathrm{ref}}(w))\,dw\right). \tag{7.12} \end{equation}(7.12) Also write Pv=P(v)P_v=P(v), as in the coefficient class (6.29). Multiplying a solution by ψ\psi changes its principal equation only where both the solution and the source are exponentially small, as shown after (7.40).

How the shear transfers energy. The pulse equation also shows where the growth of the homogeneous solution comes from. For the real amplitude t=tσht=t^h_\sigma, the constraint nΦ⋅t=0n_\Phi\cdot t=0 makes the normal term in 𝒜Φt\mathcal A_\Phi t perpendicular to tt. Also,

12ddv|t|2=−g⋅(tr(tθ,tz))−εk2|nΦ|2|t|2.\begin{equation} \frac12\frac{d}{dv}|t|^2 =-g\cdot\bigl(t_r(t_\theta,t_z)\bigr) -\varepsilon k^2|n_\Phi|^2|t|^2. \tag{7.22} \end{equation}(7.22) The first term is the exchange of energy with the base shear, while the second is viscous dissipation. The vector tr(tθ,tz)t_r(t_\theta,t_z) records the transport of azimuthal and axial momentum across a cylinder. At the representative point, write such a flux vector as T=TNN+TKKT=T_NN+T_KK. The energy transfer is −g0⋅T=−|g0|TN-g_0\cdot T=-|g_0|T_N. The covariance construction also fixes the transverse component TKT_K. Both components of the covariance must therefore match the prescribed momentum flux.

Viscosity remains a leading-order term in the pulse equation. With viscosity equal to one, the base velocity and radial length give a Reynolds number of order q−hq^{-h}. The carrier wavelength is Q/k≍Q1/2+h/2\sqrt{Q}/k\asymp Q^{1/2+h/2}, while the physical amplitude of the leading oscillations built below is of order Q−Aε=Q−1/2−h/2Q^{-A}\sqrt{\varepsilon}=Q^{-1/2-h/2}, apart from powers of S*S_*. The powers of QQ cancel in their product. Thus εk2≍1\varepsilon k^2\asymp 1 throughout the correction process in the pulse equation.

7.3 The covariance of the leading oscillations and its linearization

The two real homogeneous pulses t±ht^h_\pm from Lemma 7.4 give two covariance directions in each slow box. Proposition 7.5 chooses their scalar amplitudes a±a_\pm so that a positive combination of those directions equals the leading stress. This subsection computes the two covariances, solves for the squared amplitudes, and then differentiates that relation. The differentiated relation gives signed stress corrections through ℒ\mathcal L from Proposition 7.6.

Recall the angular and auxiliary averages in (3.7), with normalized Haar measure on the auxiliary torus. Take these averages at fixed slow variables, before evaluating at the physical phase map. For real velocity fields w,vw,v on the extended domain, write wtan=(wθ,wz)w_{\mathrm{tan}}=(w_\theta,w_z).

The product wrwtanw_rw_{\mathrm{tan}} records radial transport of azimuthal and axial momentum. At each fixed slow point, define the covariance 𝒞(w)\mathcal C(w) and the symmetric cross term ℬ(w,v)\mathcal B(w,v) by

Expanding the product gives D𝒞(w)[v]=ℬ(w,v)D\mathcal C(w)[v]=\mathcal B(w,v).

Write β=(ℓ,a)\beta=(\ell,a) for a slow box and γ=(β,σ)\gamma=(\beta,\sigma) for one of its two rectangle labels. The two signs use the same slow cutoff, ηβ=η(β,+)=η(β,−)\eta_\beta=\eta_{(\beta,+)}=\eta_{(\beta,-)}. The squared partition therefore sums over β\beta, counting each box once. On the slow neighborhood of β\beta, define

bσ=χg(ξg)ψ(v)tσhcos⁡(kΦσ),σ∈{+,−},b_\sigma=\chi_g(\xi_g)\psi(v)t^h_\sigma\cos(k\Phi_\sigma), \qquad \sigma\in\{+,-\}, and extend it by zero outside the auxiliary rectangle with that sign. The factors χg,ψ\chi_g,\psi make this extension smooth. The field bσb_\sigma contains neither the slow cutoff ηβ\eta_\beta nor a scalar amplitude. The auxiliary supports for the two signs are disjoint.

Let 𝖧=[𝒞(b+)∣𝒞(b−)]\mathsf H=[\mathcal C(b_+)\mid\mathcal C(b_-)]. This is a real 2×22\times 2 matrix that depends on the slow point, and its columns use the component order (rθ,rz)(r\theta,rz). For any real numbers a+,a−a_+,a_-, the disjoint supports give 𝒞(a+b++a−b−)=𝖧(a+2,a−2)T\mathcal C(a_+b_++a_-b_-)=\mathsf H(a_+^2,a_-^2)^T. The stresses produced by these two waves are therefore exactly the nonnegative combinations of its two columns. The strict cone condition will make the two coefficients for the leading stress positive; their square roots define the real amplitudes of the waves.

7.4 Exact curls, the tails left over, and the covariance remainder.

For the harmonic velocity tmeikmΦt_m e^{ikm\Phi}, the condition nΦ⋅tm=0n_\Phi\cdot t_m=0 says that the amplitude is orthogonal to the phase gradient, and this cancels the leading term in its divergence. Derivatives of the amplitude tmt_m still contribute. Taking the full curl of the vector potential Am=CmeikmΦA_m=C_m e^{ikm\Phi} in (7.38), rather than keeping only that leading term, gives the corrected amplitude tm+rmt_m+r_m needed for exact incompressibility. Differentiating the exponential gives the amplitude tmt_m, while differentiating the potential coefficient CmC_m and the cylindrical frame gives rmr_m. This subsection first estimates rmr_m in Lemma 7.7, then estimates the temporal cutoff residual in (7.40). This is the unused part of the source, multiplied by one minus the time cutoff, plus the time derivative of that cutoff multiplied by the pulse amplitude. The subsection finally finds the covariance of a stress increment built from the actual velocities in Corollary 7.8.

For a normalized potential A=(Ar,Aθ,Az)A=(A_r,A_\theta,A_z), define

curl⁡*A=(R−1∂θAz−DzAθ,DzAr−DrAz,(Dr+R−1)Aθ−R−1∂θAr).\begin{equation} \operatorname{curl}_* A =\bigl(R^{-1}\partial_\theta A_z-D_zA_\theta, D_zA_r-D_rA_z, (D_r+R^{-1})A_\theta-R^{-1}\partial_\theta A_r\bigr). \tag{7.37} \end{equation}(7.37) The normalized derivatives already include the chain-rule terms that appear when the potential is evaluated at (6.3). This means that curl⁡*A\operatorname{curl}_* A is the normalized physical curl of the evaluated potential.

Fix a label, a nonzero integer mm, and a harmonic coefficient tm∈𝖶αt_m\in \mathsf W_\alpha that does not depend on θ\theta and satisfies nΦ⋅tm=0n_\Phi\cdot t_m=0. Cm=inΦ×tmkm|nΦ|2,Am=CmeikmΦ,curl⁡*Am=(tm+rm)eikmΦ.\begin{equation} C_m=\frac{i\,n_\Phi\times t_m}{km|n_\Phi|^2}, \qquad A_m=C_m e^{ikm\Phi}, \qquad \operatorname{curl}_*A_m=(t_m+r_m)e^{ikm\Phi}. \tag{7.38} \end{equation}(7.38) The last identity defines rmr_m as the difference between the full curl amplitude and the prescribed transverse amplitude. Lemma 7.7.

For every α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} and every nonzero integer mm, let tm∈𝖶αt_m\in \mathsf W_\alpha satisfy nΦ⋅tm=0n_\Phi\cdot t_m=0. ikmnΦ⋅am=−((Dr+R−1)(am)r+Dz(am)z),nΦ⋅am∈𝖶α+1/2−κs.\begin{equation} ikm\,n_\Phi\cdot a_m =-\bigl((D_r+R^{-1})(a_m)_r+D_z(a_m)_z\bigr), \qquad n_\Phi\cdot a_m\in \mathsf W_{\alpha+1/2-\kappa_s}. \tag{7.39} \end{equation}(7.39) The physical potentials and pressures come from the chart versions by multiplying them by Q1/2−AQ^{1/2-A} and Q−2AQ^{-2A}, respectively.

7.4.0.1 The temporal cutoff and its residual.

For the solution in Proposition 7.2, set t̂m=ψtm\widehat t_m=\psi t_m and π̂m=ψπm\widehat\pi_m=\psi\pi_m, then apply Lemma 7.7 to t̂m\widehat t_m. Wherever either term is left, |v−Ls/2|≥Ls/5|v-L_s/2|\geq L_s/5. Equation (7.16) then adds a factor S*Ce−cS*S_*^C e^{-cS_*} to every estimate for a fixed coefficient derivative. During the iteration, fmeikmΦf_m e^{ikm\Phi} is an actual supported harmonic source whose extension by zero is smooth, so this local identity also describes the part left uncancelled in the global residual.

At any fixed correction stage, changing a fixed derivative estimate to physical variables introduces a fixed power of Q−1Q^{-1} and a polynomial in S*S_*. Since S*=ℓ2S_*=\ell^2, Q=2−ℓQ=2^{-\ell}, and q≍Qq\asymp Q, every fixed choice of M,C,NM,C,N satisfies

q−NQ−MS*Ce−cS*≤CNexp⁡(−cℓ2+(M+N)ℓlog⁡2+2Clog⁡ℓ)→0.q^{-N}Q^{-M}S_*^C e^{-cS_*} \leq C_N\exp\bigl(-c\ell^2+(M+N)\ell\log 2+2C\log\ell\bigr) \longrightarrow 0. So every resulting physical derivative is O(qN)O(q^N) for every fixed NN. Later corrections keep these terms as separate additive flat residuals. The same argument handles the homogeneous cutoff tails. The pressure coefficient still satisfies π̂m∈𝖶α+1/2\widehat\pi_m\in \mathsf W_{\alpha+1/2}, while the exact velocity amplitude is t̂m+r̂m\widehat t_m+\widehat r_m, with r̂m∈𝖶α+1/2−κs\widehat r_m\in \mathsf W_{\alpha+1/2-\kappa_s}.

7.4.0.2 Covariance of the actual velocities.

The linear covariance inverse was defined at the fixed primary wave. During the iteration, its increment is added to a divergence-free wave field that already includes earlier corrections, and the new increment has a curl remainder of its own. The exact expansion below picks out the prescribed stress increment. It also keeps the interaction with earlier corrections, the interaction with the new curl remainder, and the square of the new velocity.

Corollary 7.8.

Fix α,ρ∈ℝ\alpha,\rho\in\mathbb{R}, and use the normalized representatives from (7.35). Suppose UU is a real divergence-free wave field, including its curl remainders, with

U=W0as+E,U∈𝖶1/2,E∈𝖶ρ.U=W_0^{\mathrm{as}}+E, \qquad U\in \mathsf W_{1/2}, \qquad E\in \mathsf W_\rho. Let Σ(R,Z,T)∈𝖬α\Sigma(R,Z,T)\in \mathsf M_\alpha be a real two-vector that does not depend on the angular or auxiliary variables. Apply Lemma 7.7 to the signed amplitudes ℒasΣ\mathcal L^{\mathrm{as}}\Sigma. This gives the divergence-free increment V=ℒasΣ+RV=\mathcal L^{\mathrm{as}}\Sigma+R, where R∈𝖶α−κsR\in \mathsf W_{\alpha-\kappa_s} is its curl remainder. Then

𝒞(U+V)−𝒞(U)=Σ+ℬ(E,ℒasΣ)+ℬ(U,R)+𝒞(V).\begin{equation} \mathcal C(U+V)-\mathcal C(U) =\Sigma+\mathcal B(E,\mathcal L^{\mathrm{as}}\Sigma) +\mathcal B(U,R)+\mathcal C(V). \tag{7.41} \end{equation}(7.41) The three remainder terms satisfy

ℬ(E,ℒasΣ)∈𝖬ρ+α−1/2,ℬ(U,R)∈𝖬α+1/2−κs,𝒞(V)∈𝖬2α−1.\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal B(E,\mathcal L^{\mathrm{as}}\Sigma)&\in \mathsf M_{\rho+\alpha-1/2},\\ \mathcal B(U,R)&\in \mathsf M_{\alpha+1/2-\kappa_s},\\ \mathcal C(V)&\in \mathsf M_{2\alpha-1}. \end{aligned} \tag{7.42} \end{equation}(7.42) Taking the radial divergence of any one of these remainder terms lowers the ε\varepsilon exponent by no more than another κs\kappa_s.

Proof.

Expand the quadratic map and use ℬ(W0as,ℒasΣ)=Σ\mathcal B(W_0^{\mathrm{as}},\mathcal L^{\mathrm{as}}\Sigma)=\Sigma. This gives

𝒞(U+V)−𝒞(U)=ℬ(U,V)+𝒞(V)=ℬ(W0as,ℒasΣ)+ℬ(E,ℒasΣ)+ℬ(U,R)+𝒞(V)=Σ+ℬ(E,ℒasΣ)+ℬ(U,R)+𝒞(V).\begin{align*} \mathcal C(U+V)-\mathcal C(U) &=\mathcal B(U,V)+\mathcal C(V)\\ &=\mathcal B(W_0^{\mathrm{as}},\mathcal L^{\mathrm{as}}\Sigma) +\mathcal B(E,\mathcal L^{\mathrm{as}}\Sigma)+\mathcal B(U,R)+\mathcal C(V)\\ &=\Sigma+\mathcal B(E,\mathcal L^{\mathrm{as}}\Sigma) +\mathcal B(U,R)+\mathcal C(V). \end{align*} The bounds for ℬ(E,ℒasΣ)\mathcal B(E,\mathcal L^{\mathrm{as}}\Sigma) and ℬ(U,R)\mathcal B(U,R) come from multiplying the stated classes. Since κs<1/2\kappa_s<1/2, it follows that V∈𝖶α−1/2V\in \mathsf W_{\alpha-1/2}, and so 𝒞(V)∈𝖬2α−1\mathcal C(V)\in \mathsf M_{2\alpha-1}. This proves (7.41) and (7.42) without placing any positivity condition on an accumulated stress. The claim about radial divergence follows from (6.32); the cylindrical terms of order zero cause no further loss in the exponent. ◻

8 Compactly supported corrections to the mean

The wave construction in Section 7 gives pulses whose averaged covariance produces the leading stress target in (7.26). It also gives an inverse for the principal equation of every nonzero angular harmonic in Proposition 7.2. The residual’s angular mean, meaning its average over the physical angle, still needs to be corrected. This mean contains quadratic products of the waves, and it can depend on the auxiliary torus even though it does not depend on the physical angle, as Proposition 8.1 shows. This section builds the pressure, tangential stresses, and divergence-free velocity increments needed to correct it. All of them are supported inside the active annulus; see Proposition 8.3 and Corollary 8.5.

There are two different inversion problems. For an auxiliary-averaged source, a compactly supported solution φ\varphi of (Dr+e/R)φ=f(D_r+e/R)\varphi=f, with e∈{0,1,2}e\in\{0,1,2\}, can exist only when ∫RefdR=0\int R^e f\,dR=0; see Lemma 8.2. For a source that depends on the auxiliary torus, the fast time derivative can be inverted only when the source has zero auxiliary average at each slow point, as Lemma 8.6 explains. The section first derives the mean momentum equations in Proposition 8.1 and builds the radial inverse in Lemma 8.2, including the remainder that appears when its source depends on the torus. It then uses that inverse for pressure and divergence-free axial increments in Proposition 8.3, and for tangential stresses in Corollary 8.5. The integrated equations in (8.16) pick out three scalar defects, 𝒫,𝒥θ,𝒥z\mathcal P,\mathcal J_\theta,\mathcal J_z, defined in Equations (8.12) and (8.15). A final linear map chooses five velocity coefficients so that their linear changes cancel these three defects while two velocity moments stay unchanged; this is Lemma 8.7. Lemma 8.8 calculates the nonlinear changes explicitly. The correction cycle in Proposition 9.6 uses all these constructions after every wave update.

Any radial integral without stated limits runs from zero to infinity. The averaging and projection conventions are the ones in Equations (3.7) and (3.9). Recall that ⟨⋅⟩θ\langle\,\cdot\,\rangle_\theta takes the angular average of each cylindrical component, while ⟨⋅⟩Y\langle\,\cdot\,\rangle_Y takes the Haar average on the auxiliary torus from Lemma 6.2, and f∘=f−⟨f⟩Yf^\circ=f-\langle f\rangle_Y. So a field can be angularly invariant and still depend on that torus. The coefficient classes 𝖬α\mathsf M_\alpha and 𝖲α\mathsf S_\alpha are the classes from Definition 6.4; their estimates hold at every fixed derivative order. Unless physical variables are written out, the variables and operators are the normalized chart versions from (6.6).

8.1 Momentum equations in divergence form and integral constraints.

Here, divergence form means writing the transport terms as radial and axial derivatives of momentum fluxes, with the extra terms required by cylindrical coordinates kept beside them. This subsection derives the mean momentum equations in divergence form in Proposition 8.1, and states the two velocity moments in (8.2) that the corrections must leave unchanged. Radial integration of these equations shows which compactly supported corrections are possible, as Proposition 8.4 and Corollary 8.5 explain. Writing the equations in divergence form also shows the boundary contributions explicitly. The calculation keeps the quadratic products of the actual divergence-free field ww, including its curl remainders, as shown in (8.1). In a common chart, using the normalized operators from (6.6), the actual velocity splits as

u=(b+β,V+v,G+γ)+w,⟨w⟩θ=0,Wab=⟨wawb⟩θ.\begin{equation} u=(b+\beta,V+v,G+\gamma)+w, \qquad \langle w\rangle_\theta=0, \qquad W_{ab}=\langle w_aw_b\rangle_\theta. \tag{8.1} \end{equation}(8.1) Here (b,V,G)(b,V,G) is the slow base, (β,v,γ)(\beta,v,\gamma) is its correction that does not depend on the physical angle, and ww is the sum of the divergence-free fields made by taking curls of the wave potentials. The indices in WabW_{ab} run over a,b∈{r,θ,z}a,b\in\{r,\theta,z\}, so WW includes every curl remainder. The correction components and WW extend smoothly by zero outside the active shell. The mean correction is divergence-free, which means (Dr+R−1)β+Dzγ=0(D_r+R^{-1})\beta+D_z\gamma=0, and it must satisfy the two integral constraints

Mθ:=∫0∞R2⟨v⟩YdR=0,Mz:=∫0∞R⟨γ⟩YdR=0.\begin{equation} M_\theta:=\int_0^\infty R^2\langle v\rangle_Y\,dR=0, \qquad M_z:=\int_0^\infty R\langle\gamma\rangle_Y\,dR=0. \tag{8.2} \end{equation}(8.2) These two identities hold at every (Z,T)(Z,T). Up to normalization, they say that the auxiliary-averaged correction has zero angular-momentum moment and zero axial-flux integral. The base is handled separately. Compactly supported azimuthal potentials leave the axial-flux constraint unchanged, and the finite-dimensional moment correction leaves both constraints unchanged.

Let pmp_m be the perturbation’s mean pressure. Put Δ0=Dr2+R−1Dr+Dz2\Delta_0=D_r^2+R^{-1}D_r+D_z^2 and Σa=Q2A𝒯phys,a\Sigma_a=Q^{2A}\mathcal T_{\mathrm{phys},a} for a=θ,za=\theta,z, where the full residual stress tensor is the one in (5.41).

Proposition 8.1.

Let uu have the divergence-free decomposition in (8.1), with slow base (b,V,G)(b,V,G), correction (β,v,γ)(\beta,v,\gamma) independent of the physical angle, and ⟨w⟩θ=0\langle w\rangle_\theta=0. Let pmp_m be its pressure correction independent of the physical angle, and let Σa=Q2A𝒯phys,a\Sigma_a=Q^{2A}\mathcal T_{\mathrm{phys},a} be the normalized components of the base stress from (5.41). Keep the base’s flat residual as a separate additive error. All its derivatives of every fixed order vanish faster than every power of qq. Then the angular mean of the rest of the normalized residual is (Drpm−gr,Eθ,Ez)(D_rp_m-g_r,E_\theta,E_z), where

Eθ=𝔱*v+(Dr+2/R)(bv+βV+βv+Wrθ)+Dz(Gv+Vγ+γv+Wzθ)−ε(Δ0−R−2)v−(Dr+2/R)Σθ,Ez=𝔱*γ+(Dr+1/R)(bγ+βG+βγ+Wrz)+Dz(2Gγ+γ2+Wzz+pm)−εΔ0γ−(Dr+1/R)Σz,gr=−𝔱*β−(Dr+1/R)(2bβ+β2+Wrr)−Dz(bγ+Gβ+βγ+Wzr)+(2Vv+v2+Wθθ)/R+ε(Δ0−R−2)β.\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} E_\theta={}&\mathfrak t_*v+(D_r+2/R)(bv+\beta V+\beta v+W_{r\theta})\\ &+D_z(Gv+V\gamma+\gamma v+W_{z\theta}) -\varepsilon(\Delta_0-R^{-2})v-(D_r+2/R)\Sigma_\theta,\\ E_z={}&\mathfrak t_*\gamma+(D_r+1/R)(b\gamma+\beta G+\beta\gamma+W_{rz})\\ &+D_z(2G\gamma+\gamma^2+W_{zz}+p_m)-\varepsilon\Delta_0\gamma-(D_r+1/R)\Sigma_z,\\ g_r={}&-\mathfrak t_*\beta-(D_r+1/R)(2b\beta+\beta^2+W_{rr})\\ &-D_z(b\gamma+G\beta+\beta\gamma+W_{zr}) +(2Vv+v^2+W_{\theta\theta})/R+\varepsilon(\Delta_0-R^{-2})\beta. \end{aligned} \tag{8.3} \end{equation}(8.3)

Proof.

Incompressibility lets the transport terms be written in divergence form. For the cylindrical components of any divergence-free field, the three transport expressions are

(u⋅∇u)r=(Dr+1/R)ur2+R−1∂θ(uθur)+Dz(uzur)−uθ2/R,(u⋅∇u)θ=(Dr+2/R)(uruθ)+R−1∂θuθ2+Dz(uzuθ),(u⋅∇u)z=(Dr+1/R)(uruz)+R−1∂θ(uθuz)+Dzuz2.\begin{align*} (u\cdot\nabla u)_r &=(D_r+1/R)u_r^2+R^{-1}\partial_\theta(u_\theta u_r)+D_z(u_z u_r)-u_\theta^2/R,\\ (u\cdot\nabla u)_\theta &=(D_r+2/R)(u_r u_\theta)+R^{-1}\partial_\theta u_\theta^2+D_z(u_z u_\theta),\\ (u\cdot\nabla u)_z &=(D_r+1/R)(u_r u_z)+R^{-1}\partial_\theta(u_\theta u_z)+D_z u_z^2. \end{align*} The turning of the cylindrical frame produces the centrifugal term in the first row and the extra uruθ/Ru_ru_\theta/R in the second. Any angular derivative integrates to zero, and so does any product with exactly one factor of ww. Once the pure base terms are subtracted, the fluxes left are the ones in (8.3). The angular-derivative terms in the vector Laplacian also have zero angular average. This leaves Δ0−R−2\Delta_0-R^{-2} in the radial and angular components and Δ0\Delta_0 in the axial component. By (5.41), the residual stress tensor contributes the two radial divergences displayed in (8.3). The pulse tails left out have nonzero angular harmonics, so their angular mean is zero. The calculation keeps the full covariance of the divergence-free wave field, including all its curl remainders. ◻

8.2 A compactly supported primitive for the cylindrical weights.

This subsection builds a radial primitive by integrating in the radial direction along the matching torus path, and keeps its support inside the active shell; see Lemma 8.2. A direct radial integral may still be nonzero after the source support has ended. To stop that from happening, subtract its full radial integral multiplied by a fixed cutoff, and keep the error created by this subtraction. After evaluation at the phase, the radial derivative also differentiates the auxiliary variable in (6.4), so both integrals must follow the matching path on the torus. That path is included in the physical definition below.

Start with the radial operations in physical variables, keeping (z,t)(z,t) and the independent angular variable fixed. Choose a slow cutoff χm(X)\chi_m(X) that is zero on an inner collar, equals one on an outer collar, and changes only in a fixed interior part of the active shell. Let g(r,z,t,Y)g(r,z,t,Y) be a smooth source that is periodic in YY and extends smoothly by zero outside that shell. Set

ℐg(r,Y)=∫0rg(r′,Y+((r′)dr−rdr)vr)dr′,𝒥g(r,Y)=∫0∞g(r′,Y+((r′)dr−rdr)vr)dr′,ℐcg=ℐg−χm𝒥g.\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal I g(r,Y) &=\int_0^r g\bigl(r',Y+((r')^{d_r}-r^{d_r})v_r\bigr)\,dr',\\ \mathcal J g(r,Y) &=\int_0^\infty g\bigl(r',Y+((r')^{d_r}-r^{d_r})v_r\bigr)\,dr',\\ \mathcal I_c g&=\mathcal I g-\chi_m\mathcal J g. \end{aligned} \tag{8.4} \end{equation}(8.4) The shift in YY follows the radial phase map while the physical variables (z,t)(z,t) stay fixed. Below the shell, ℐg=0\mathcal I g=0; above it, ℐg=𝒥g\mathcal I g=\mathcal J g. It follows that ℐcg\mathcal I_c g is zero when X≤XaX\leq X_a and when X≥XbX\geq X_b, and it extends smoothly by zero across both radial edges. The subtraction creates an error supported where χm\chi_m changes, and that error is kept in the radial equation.

For the normalized operators, use a common torus y=Yi0y=Y_{i_0} and set M=Λgi0Qdr/2M=\Lambda_g^{i_0}Q^{d_r}/2. At fixed (Z,T)(Z,T), the same symbols mean

ℐg(R,y)=∫0Rg(R′,y+M((R′)dr−Rdr)vr)dR′,𝒥g(R,y)=∫0∞g(R′,y+M((R′)dr−Rdr)vr)dR′,ℐcg=ℐg−χm𝒥g.\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal I g(R,y) &=\int_0^R g\bigl(R',y+M((R')^{d_r}-R^{d_r})v_r\bigr)\,dR',\\ \mathcal J g(R,y) &=\int_0^\infty g\bigl(R',y+M((R')^{d_r}-R^{d_r})v_r\bigr)\,dR',\\ \mathcal I_c g&=\mathcal I g-\chi_m\mathcal J g. \end{aligned} \tag{8.5} \end{equation}(8.5) Here χm=χm(QR2/(2q))\chi_m=\chi_m(QR^2/(2q)) is how the fixed physical cutoff appears in the chart. For e∈{0,1,2}e\in\{0,1,2\}, define

𝒟e=Dr+e/R,𝖳ef=R−eℐc(Ref),𝒜ef=R−e(∂Rχm)𝒥(Ref).\begin{equation} \mathcal D_e=D_r+e/R, \qquad \mathsf T_e f=R^{-e}\mathcal I_c(R^e f), \qquad \mathcal A_e f=R^{-e}(\partial_R\chi_m)\mathcal J(R^e f). \tag{8.6} \end{equation}(8.6) At matching physical and chart points, where r=QRr=\sqrt Q\,R, the normalization is

f*=Qafphys,Qa−1/2r−eℐc,phys(refphys)=R−eℐc(Ref*)=𝖳ef*.f_*=Q^a f_{\mathrm{phys}}, \qquad Q^{a-1/2}r^{-e}\mathcal I_{c,\mathrm{phys}}(r^e f_{\mathrm{phys}}) =R^{-e}\mathcal I_c(R^e f_*)=\mathsf T_e f_*. Here ℐc,phys\mathcal I_{c,\mathrm{phys}} is the physical operator defined above. The term 𝒜ef\mathcal A_e f is the cutoff remainder created by making the primitive compactly supported.

The inverse must keep the source’s decay order. The next lemma assumes that the source is multiplied by the stated power of the radial variable, averaged over the auxiliary torus, and then integrated over the full radial line. At every fixed value of the other two slow variables, the result must be zero. Under that exact condition, the cutoff remainder must also be flat. The lemma gives both estimates.

Lemma 8.2.

Fix a correction stage jj, an exponent α\alpha, a band, its common torus y=Yi0y=Y_{i_0}, and e∈{0,1,2}e\in\{0,1,2\}. Let f∈𝖬αf\in \mathsf M_\alpha be a smooth scalar coefficient. The input’s extension by zero includes derivatives of the moving shell, so taking derivatives creates no boundary terms.

To estimate the cutoff term still left, use the cancellation in the full radial integral. Haar measure does not change under translation, so ⟨𝒥g⟩Y=∫⟨g⟩YdR\langle\mathcal Jg\rangle_Y=\int\langle g\rangle_Y\,dR. Under the weighted moment condition, this is zero for g=Refg=R^ef. It gives

Whenever the weighted mean integral is zero, the inverse is exact apart from a flat cutoff remainder. This flatness uses estimates at every fixed derivative order. 8.3 Reconstructing the pressure and making divergence-free velocity corrections.

This subsection applies the radial inverse from Lemma 8.2 first to the pressure pmp_m, then to an azimuthal vector potential that produces a divergence-free velocity increment; see Proposition 8.3. The axial component of that increment equals the prescribed source γd\gamma_d, apart from the cutoff remainder in (8.14). The pressure source may have a nonzero radial integral after its auxiliary average is taken. Subtracting a fixed bump times that integral separates out the obstruction, and the source left over can then be integrated with compact support, as in (8.12).

ρphys(r,z,t)=q−1/2ρ̂(r/q),ρ=Q1/2ρphys.\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}(r,z,t)=q^{-1/2}\widehat\rho(r/\sqrt q), \qquad \rho=Q^{1/2}\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}. The operator 𝖳0\mathsf T_0 reconstructs the pressure, while 𝖳1\mathsf T_1 reconstructs an azimuthal vector potential. The operators 𝖳1\mathsf T_1 and 𝖳2\mathsf T_2 also recover the radial fluxes of axial and azimuthal momentum. Write Ψ\Psi for the azimuthal coefficient of the vector potential. With a star marking a normalized representative, the physical normalizations are

u*=QAuphys,g*=Q2A+1/2gphys,p*=Q2Apphys,Ψ*=QA−1/2Ψphys,ρ*=Q1/2ρphys.\begin{equation} \begin{gathered} u_*=Q^A u_{\mathrm{phys}},\qquad g_*=Q^{2A+1/2}g_{\mathrm{phys}},\qquad p_*=Q^{2A}p_{\mathrm{phys}},\\ \Psi_*=Q^{A-1/2}\Psi_{\mathrm{phys}},\qquad \rho_*=Q^{1/2}\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}. \end{gathered} \tag{8.11} \end{equation}(8.11) In particular, Q2Aℐc,physgphys=ℐcg*Q^{2A}\mathcal I_{c,\mathrm{phys}}g_{\mathrm{phys}}=\mathcal I_cg_*. When the ε\varepsilon exponent is said to be preserved, it refers to these normalized representatives and already includes the length of integration.

8.4 The three compatibility defects in the integrated equations.

This subsection finds the integral defects left by the pressure reconstruction in (8.13) and by the two tangential equations in (8.3). These defects are the quantities that must be removed before the required compactly supported corrections can exist. Tangential stresses are then built so that their radial divergences cancel the auxiliary-averaged residuals apart from two explicit bump terms; see Corollary 8.5. The pressure reconstruction leaves the integral 𝒫\mathcal P from (8.12) to be corrected. In the same way, the auxiliary averages of the tangential residuals must have zero weighted radial integrals before compactly supported stresses can represent them, by Lemma 8.2. The moment constraints in (8.2) remove the time terms and the axial-viscosity terms from these integrals. The axial fluxes left after that give two more defects, as Equations (8.15) and (8.16) show.

Along with 𝒫\mathcal P from (8.12), define the two flux defects and the second radial moment cρc_\rho of ρ\rho by

𝒥θ=∫R2⟨Gv+Vγ+γv+Wzθ⟩YdR,𝒥z=∫R⟨2Gγ+γ2+Wzz⟩YdR−12∫R2⟨gr⟩YdR,cρ=12∫R2ρdR.\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal J_\theta &=\int R^2\langle Gv+V\gamma+\gamma v+W_{z\theta}\rangle_Y\,dR,\\ \mathcal J_z &=\int R\langle2G\gamma+\gamma^2+W_{zz}\rangle_Y\,dR -\frac12\int R^2\langle g_r\rangle_Y\,dR, &c_\rho&=\frac12\int R^2\rho\,dR. \end{aligned} \tag{8.15} \end{equation}(8.15)

Proposition 8.4.

Let (β,v,γ)(\beta,v,\gamma) and ww be the smooth corrections from (8.1), supported in the shell. Suppose that the two moments in (8.2) are zero at every (Z,T)(Z,T), and reconstruct pmp_m from their radial source grg_r by (8.12). For the residual components Eθ,EzE_\theta,E_z from (8.3) and the defects 𝒥θ,𝒥z,cρ\mathcal J_\theta,\mathcal J_z,c_\rho from (8.15),

∫R2⟨Eθ⟩YdR=ε∂Z𝒥θ,∫R⟨Ez⟩YdR=ε∂Z(𝒥z+cρ𝒫).\begin{equation} \int R^2\langle E_\theta\rangle_Y\,dR =\varepsilon\partial_Z\mathcal J_\theta, \qquad \int R\langle E_z\rangle_Y\,dR =\varepsilon\partial_Z(\mathcal J_z+c_\rho\mathcal P). \tag{8.16} \end{equation}(8.16)

After auxiliary averaging, DrD_r becomes ∂R\partial_R, and 𝔱*\mathfrak t_* becomes −ε∂T-\varepsilon\partial_T. Multiply each radial divergence in (8.3), including the one from the residual stress tensor, by its stated weight and integrate. Each one becomes a term at the endpoints, and compact support makes those terms zero. Two integrations by parts make the radial viscous integrals zero.

∫R2(vRR+R−1vR−R−2v)dR=(2−1−1)∫vdR=0,\int R^2(v_{RR}+R^{-1}v_R-R^{-2}v)\,dR =(2-1-1)\int v\,dR=0, ∫R(γRR+R−1γR)dR=−∫γRdR+∫γRdR=0.\int R(\gamma_{RR}+R^{-1}\gamma_R)\,dR =-\int\gamma_R\,dR+\int\gamma_R\,dR=0. The compactly supported pressure reconstruction fixes the pressure moment as follows.

∫R⟨pm⟩YdR=−12∫R2∂R⟨pm⟩YdR=−12∫R2⟨gr⟩YdR+cρ𝒫.\int R\langle p_m\rangle_Y\,dR =-\frac12\int R^2\partial_R\langle p_m\rangle_Y\,dR =-\frac12\int R^2\langle g_r\rangle_Y\,dR+c_\rho\mathcal P. The moments in physical variables and their normalized representatives are related by

The two tangential residual moments are therefore axial derivatives of 𝒥θ\mathcal J_\theta and 𝒥z+cρ𝒫\mathcal J_z+c_\rho\mathcal P. ∫R2(⟨Eθ⟩Y−σθε∂Z𝒥θ)dR=0,∫R(⟨Ez⟩Y−σzε∂Z(𝒥z+cρ𝒫))dR=0.\begin{align*} \int R^2\bigl(\langle E_\theta\rangle_Y -\sigma_\theta\varepsilon\partial_Z\mathcal J_\theta\bigr)\,dR&=0,\\ \int R\bigl(\langle E_z\rangle_Y -\sigma_z\varepsilon\partial_Z(\mathcal J_z+c_\rho\mathcal P)\bigr)\,dR&=0. \end{align*} Both sources are independent of the auxiliary variable. 8.5 Inverting the auxiliary-time derivative on zero-mean functions.

Corollary 8.5 reduces the auxiliary-averaged correction to the three integral defects and a compactly supported stress. The part of the mean residual left after its auxiliary average is removed, (Eθ∘,Ez∘)(E_\theta^\circ,E_z^\circ), has zero auxiliary average at every slow point by (3.9). Its correction comes from the fast time derivative. The Fourier multiplier for that derivative is invertible at every nonzero torus frequency by (6.7). The axial velocity increment is then made from its azimuthal potential through (8.14), which keeps the velocity incompressible.

Recall from Equations (6.4) and (6.6) that Nabs=vt⋅∂YN_{\mathrm{abs}}=v_t\cdot\partial_Y acts on the original auxiliary coordinate. On a common torus y=Yi0y=Y_{i_0}, the normalized fast time derivative is ci0Ni0c_{i_0}N_{i_0}, where Ni0=vt⋅∂yN_{i_0}=v_t\cdot\partial_y and ci0=Tgi0Q1+hc_{i_0}=T_g^{i_0}Q^{1+h}. The normalized physical time derivative splits as 𝔱*=−ε∂T+ci0Ni0\mathfrak t_*=-\varepsilon\partial_T+c_{i_0}N_{i_0}. Its slow part −ε∂T-\varepsilon\partial_T differentiates the coefficient’s explicit dependence on time while yy stays fixed. 8.6 A five-dimensional correction that preserves the moment constraints.

At this point, there are inverses for the pressure in Proposition 8.3, the auxiliary-averaged tangential residual in Corollary 8.5, and the part with zero auxiliary average in Lemma 8.6. This subsection corrects their linear changes by adding a velocity increment that also leaves the two constraints in (8.2) unchanged. Three azimuthal coefficients and two axial coefficients solve the five equations in (8.25).

On the reserved mean patch, Proposition 5.5 says that the background still follows the power law (4.30). This form turns the equations into separate power moments of bumps with compact support. Lemma 8.7 first builds one fixed linear map that works for any target values. Lemma 8.8 then finds the terms that remain when those targets are the defects in the current fields.

For x=r/q∈Imx=r/\sqrt q\in I_m, normalizing the velocity at qq gives the base

This means that (8.24) holds for the summed base used in the balances. The fixed parameter λ\lambda is positive.

8.7 Recomputing the fields and matching them between charts.

This subsection gives the order for recomputing the residuals and defects in Equations (8.3), (8.12), and (8.15) after a mean correction. It also checks that the constructions match between charts, using Equations (8.4) and (8.23) and Lemma 6.2. Each correction changes the quadratic fluxes, so the next source has to be computed from the updated divergence-free velocity. A cutoff remainder whose auxiliary average is zero can have a nonzero average after multiplication by another term. Its contributions to the pressure and to the compatibility integrals in Equations (8.3) and (8.15) therefore have to be kept in the next step.

Fix the base coefficients and the stress. An actual velocity tuple (β,v,γ,w)(\beta,v,\gamma,w) then determines the pressure and the mean residuals in this order.

  1. Using the full wave velocities, form Wab=⟨wawb⟩θW_{ab}=\langle w_aw_b\rangle_\theta. Then define grg_r by the third row of (8.3).

  2. Define 𝒫=∫⟨gr⟩YdR\mathcal P=\int\langle g_r\rangle_Y\,dR and pm=𝖳0(gr−ρ𝒫)p_m=\mathsf T_0(g_r-\rho\mathcal P).

  3. With this pressure, define Eθ,EzE_\theta,E_z by the first two rows of (8.3).

  4. Using the same velocity and radial source, define 𝒥θ,𝒥z\mathcal J_\theta,\mathcal J_z by (8.15).

Repeat these definitions after every change to the velocity. For either kind of mean update, the new tuple is

(β,v,γ,w)new=(β+Δβ,v+Δv,γ+Δγ,w).(\beta,v,\gamma,w)_{\mathrm{new}} =(\beta+\Delta\beta,v+\Delta v,\gamma+\Delta\gamma,w). For the temporal update, use the current Eθ∘,Ez∘E_\theta^\circ,E_z^\circ in (8.20). For the moment update, use the current (𝒫,𝒥θ,𝒥z)(\mathcal P,\mathcal J_\theta,\mathcal J_z) in (8.25). In both updates, Δγ\Delta\gamma means the actual axial increment from (8.14). Its cutoff remainder is therefore included before any of the products in the four definitions above are evaluated. After the moment update, Equations (8.26)–(8.27) give the recomputed defects exactly.

Proposition 9.6 and its proof give the correction cycle and the estimates for its exponents.

Because the definitions use physical variables, they match across charts. The radial integrals keep (z,t)(z,t) fixed, and q=q(z,t)q=q(z,t) keeps them from creating new dyadic bands. It is therefore possible to fix one common index on a neighborhood that contains the closures of all the supports in question. The Fourier covariance in (8.23) makes the formulas agree where the charts overlap, and the radial formulas agree because they have the same physical definition. Changing representations shifts the covering indices by only bounded amounts. The integer-valued covering indices are held fixed while derivatives are taken, and the coordinate changes preserve the derivative bounds already proved. All the estimates above hold on the same domain 0<q<q*0<q<q_*, which was fixed before the iteration. On any closed region q≥c>0q\ge c>0, including η=±1\eta=\pm 1, only finitely many bands occur. On this region, the fixed-shift integrals, the inverse Fourier transform, and the finite-dimensional moment correction preserve every one-sided derivative of the source, including the derivatives at the endpoints.

9 Improving the residual and building the local field

The wave and mean constructions from Sections 7 and 8 correct different parts of the momentum residual. This section puts them together to prove Theorem 3.1. Start with the fixed background (uB,pB)(u_B,p_B) from Proposition 5.5 and the primary fields assembled in (7.35), which Lemma 7.7 makes divergence-free. The construction must produce a local velocity ulocu_{\mathrm{loc}} whose residual and every derivative of that residual vanish to every order at the singularity, while the inner velocity growth and the exterior heat flow remain unchanged. Every correction creates new nonlinear errors. A full cycle therefore has to improve the decay before the next cycle begins.

One cycle works in the following order. Proposition 7.2 first removes the nonzero angular harmonics. Equation (7.31) then changes the primary amplitudes to adjust the averaged stress. The mean equations use (8.20) to remove the part whose auxiliary average is zero. Finally, the five-equation system (8.25) corrects the three compactly supported defects while preserving the two moment constraints. Proposition 9.6 proves that a cycle gains a fixed positive power of ε\varepsilon. Every inverse uses the same fixed background and the same primary amplitudes. This lets every finite stage live on one common domain, as Lemma 9.7 shows. Summing the stages there gives the local field in Proposition 9.9.

Table 1 collects the scales, operators, and field classes that occur repeatedly. In this section, κs=10−5\kappa_s=10^{-5}, and 𝖶α,𝖬α,𝖲α\mathsf W_\alpha,\mathsf M_\alpha,\mathsf S_\alpha have the meaning given in Section 6.4 at every derivative order. Each exponent is a power of ε=Qh\varepsilon=Q^h, with the normalization

used for those classes. At a fixed correction stage and a fixed order of amplitude differentiation, the constants, the powers of S*S_*, and the inverse powers of distance are allowed to depend on that stage and order. They are uniform in the band, label, copy, and point. The angular mean ⟨⋅⟩θ\langle\cdot\rangle_\theta and the auxiliary mean ⟨⋅⟩Y\langle\cdot\rangle_Y are different operations, both defined in (3.7). Every class estimate is an estimate for normalized chart coefficients. The factors that recover the physical velocity, pressure, and residual are Q−AQ^{-A}, Q−2AQ^{-2A}, and Q−2A−1/2Q^{-2A-1/2}, respectively. In particular, the physical fields have residual

ℛ(u,p)=∂tu+(u⋅∇)u−Δu+∇p,ℛ*=Q2A+1/2ℛ(u,p).\mathscr R(u,p)=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u-\Delta u+\nabla p, \qquad \mathscr R_*=Q^{2A+1/2}\mathscr R(u,p). The residual identities below use physical fields, while their estimates use normalized coefficients. A Cartesian space–time jet collects a field and all its Cartesian space–time derivatives up to the stated order. Equation (5.23) writes |⋅|m|\cdot|_m for the largest absolute value among them through that order.

9.1 Residual estimates for velocities built from curls

The amplitude equations (7.5) cancel the main part of a prescribed source. The physical velocity also contains the terms created by taking a curl, as Lemma 7.7 describes. Its residual contains derivatives of the amplitudes and the background as well. Equation (9.2) expands those terms. Proposition 9.1 and Lemma 9.2 first estimate the linear terms left after the main cancellation and the nonlinear interactions. Those estimates give the gains needed when Proposition 9.6 adds one correction after another.

For a fixed label, write an angular harmonic as aexp⁡(ikmΦ)a\exp(ikm\Phi), where m∈ℤ\{0}m\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\} and aa is the amplitude. Equation (7.4) defines the phase normal nΦn_\Phi, and (6.6) gives the chain-rule operators for evaluation at Y=Y(r,t)Y=Y(r,t). The background coefficients (b,V,G)(b,V,G) are the ones used in Sections 6 and 7.

For a transverse amplitude tmt_m, the potential in (7.38) gives

Here rmr_m is the correction created by taking the curl. If tm∈𝖶αt_m\in \mathsf W_\alpha, then Lemma 7.7 gives rm∈𝖶α+1/2−κsr_m\in \mathsf W_{\alpha+1/2-\kappa_s}. Here longitudinal means measured in the direction of the phase normal. Equation (7.39) estimates the scalar product with that normal for the full amplitude ama_m. This difference matters in the quadratic transport term, because the factor doing the advecting is the full divergence-free velocity.

Separate the principal linear operator, which the amplitude equation handles, from all the other transport, pressure, and viscous terms. For comparison with the residual later, write the principal operator acting on an amplitude and its pressure as

ℒm(a,π)=Q1+hNabsa+𝒦a+εk2m2|nΦ|2a+ikmnΦπ.\begin{equation} \mathscr L_m(a,\pi)=Q^{1+h}N_{\mathrm{abs}}a+\mathcal Ka +\varepsilon k^2m^2|n_\Phi|^2a+ikmn_\Phi\pi. \tag{9.1} \end{equation}(9.1) The inverse from Proposition 7.2 constructs (tm,πm)(t_m,\pi_m) so that ℒm(tm,πm)=−fm\mathscr L_m(t_m,\pi_m)=-f_m and nΦ⋅tm=0n_\Phi\cdot t_m=0, before the pulse cutoff is applied. The amplitude tmt_m does not have to extend by zero in time before that cutoff is applied.

Proposition 9.1.

Fix a label, m∈ℤ\{0}m\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}, and α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb R. Let fm∈𝖶αf_m\in \mathsf W_\alpha satisfy the support and smooth-extension assumptions in Proposition 7.2. Also assume that the source harmonic fmeikmΦf_me^{ikm\Phi} extends smoothly by zero outside the fixed local rectangle, including across the ends of its pulse. Let (tm,πm)(t_m,\pi_m) solve ℒm(tm,πm)=−fm\mathscr L_m(t_m,\pi_m)=-f_m. The same conclusion holds for a homogeneous pulse tm∈𝖶αt_m\in \mathsf W_\alpha, with fm=0f_m=0. Multiply the potential and the pressure by the pulse cutoff, then take the curl as in (7.38). After the prescribed source fmeikmΦf_me^{ikm\Phi} has been added, the normalized linear residual lies in 𝖶α+1/2−3κs\mathsf W_{\alpha+1/2-3\kappa_s}. The only terms left outside that class are additive tails from the pulse cutoff, and every Cartesian space–time derivative of each tail vanishes to infinite order as q↓0q\downarrow 0. The pressure amplitude πm\pi_m lies in 𝖶α+1/2\mathsf W_{\alpha+1/2}.

Expand the linearized residual into its principal operator (9.1) and the terms left over. For this calculation, aa is any harmonic amplitude and π\pi is its pressure amplitude. Let

The transverse-amplitude equation in Proposition 7.2 gives ℒm(tm,πm)=−fm\mathscr L_m(t_m,\pi_m)=-f_m, with πm∈𝖶α+1/2\pi_m\in \mathsf W_{\alpha+1/2}. For each kind of term in (9.2), the gain over α\alpha is listed below.

Applying the principal velocity operator to the curl correction does not change its exponent. The fast-time derivative differentiates an amplitude coefficient, and εk2=O(1)\varepsilon k^2=O(1). At every derivative order, the potential formula and these chain-rule operators give the common lower bound α+1/2−3κs\alpha+1/2-3\kappa_s for the exponents of these terms.

Apply the pulse cutoff to the potential and the pressure before taking the curl. The source left uncancelled, (1−ψ)f(1-\psi)f, and the main derivative of the pulse cutoff, ψ′t\psi't, together with its fixed multipliers, are supported where Pv≤e−cS*P_v\le e^{-cS_*}. For every fixed physical derivative, their bounds have the form CQ−MS*Pe−cS*CQ^{-M}S_*^Pe^{-cS_*}. They are therefore flat, because S*=ℓ2S_*=\ell^2 and Q=2−ℓQ=2^{-\ell}.
