The nonlinear terms need separate estimates for interactions between a wave and a mean field and for interactions between two waves. In the two-wave case, incompressibility controls the contraction of the advecting amplitude with the phase gradient.

In the next lemma, (w⋅∇*)v(w\cdot\nabla_*)v means cylindrical transport with the normalized derivatives (Dr,R−1∂θ,Dz)(D_r,R^{-1}\partial_\theta,D_z), including the terms created by differentiating the cylindrical frame. The lemma therefore estimates the normalized nonlinear residual.

Lemma 9.2.

Let ww be a wave in 𝖶α\mathsf W_\alpha. Let vv be a mean field whose tangential components lie in 𝖬μ\mathsf M_\mu and whose radial component lies in 𝖬μ+1\mathsf M_{\mu+1}. Then the nonzero harmonics of (w⋅∇*)v+(v⋅∇*)w(w\cdot\nabla_*)v+(v\cdot\nabla_*)w lie in 𝖶α+μ−1/2\mathsf W_{\alpha+\mu-1/2}.

Take two waves w,w′w,w' built from curls, with the same label and with exponents α,α′\alpha,\alpha'. The nonzero harmonics of (w⋅∇*)w′+(w′⋅∇*)w(w\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla_*)w'+(w'\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla_*)w lie in 𝖶α+α′−κs\mathsf W_{\alpha+\alpha'-\kappa_s}, and the zero harmonic lies in the mean class 𝖬α+α′−κs\mathsf M_{\alpha+\alpha'-\kappa_s}. Waves with different labels have zero product on their closed supports.

Proof.

When a mean field advects the phase of a wave, the phase derivative costs k=O(ε−1/2)k=O(\varepsilon^{-1/2}). Radial transport of the amplitude contains a radial mean factor of order μ+1\mu+1 and one DrD_r. Axial transport gains one power through DzD_z. When a wave transports a mean field, the radial cost is at most κs\kappa_s, and the cylindrical connection terms contain no derivatives. Each of these terms has at least the claimed mean–wave exponent.

Now take two harmonics with the same label. When the transport derivative falls on a′exp⁡(ikm′Φ)a'\exp(ikm'\Phi) and the advecting harmonic is aexp⁡(ikmΦ)a\exp(ikm\Phi), phase differentiation gives ikm′(a⋅nΦ)a′ikm'(a\mathbin{\cdot}n_\Phi)a'. Equation (7.39) cancels what looks like a loss of one half-power. Terms where the derivative falls on the amplitude cost at most κs\kappa_s, and the connection terms cost nothing. The pulse weights satisfy Pv2≤PvP_v^2\le P_v and their product has radial weight ζ\zeta. For a nonzero output, this is stronger than the required ζ\sqrt\zeta weight. Lemma 6.1 gives the support separation for different labels. Applying Leibniz’ rule gives every statement at each fixed order of amplitude differentiation. ◻

9.2 Sources and errors kept during the iteration

To apply Proposition 9.1 and Lemma 9.2 at one stage after another, every new source has to satisfy the support and derivative assumptions of the pulse inverse in Proposition 7.2. Mean operations can make the auxiliary support larger, so those assumptions have to be checked after a whole cycle. Equation (9.3) keeps the errors that are already flat at the singularity separate from the sources still waiting to be corrected. Even so, every nonlinear product uses the full velocity fields. The supported sources also have to stay inside the fixed enlarged rectangle. Proposition 9.3 proves all of these facts.

Use the source supports Ωγ\Omega_\gamma and the enlarged domains ℰγ+\mathcal E_\gamma^+ from (6.28). The flat term below contains the base error ℰB\mathcal E_B from (5.41), the tails caused by pulse cutoffs, and the cutoff remainders that have not been canceled. The exact mean balances can include these flat terms, because their definition always uses the full current velocity. Angular means can fill the whole auxiliary torus. The rectangle and envelope conditions below apply only to the nonzero harmonics.

The following three statements then hold.

The set ℋj\mathscr H_j depends on the finite construction, but not on the band. The coefficients satisfy

    supp⁡(fγ,m[j]|ℰγ)⊂Ωγ,fγ,m[j]∈C∞(ℰγ+;ℂ3),\operatorname{supp}(f_{\gamma,m}^{[j]}|_{\mathcal E_\gamma})\subset\Omega_\gamma, \qquad f_{\gamma,m}^{[j]}\in C^\infty(\mathcal E_\gamma^+;\mathbb C^3), and they extend smoothly by zero across the fixed slow support, the fixed transverse support, and the enlarged local torus rectangle. Let α,μ\alpha,\mu be any lower bounds for the wave and mean exponents obtained by

    fγ,m[j]∈𝖶α,⟨𝒢*[j]⟩θ∈𝖬μ.f_{\gamma,m}^{[j]}\in \mathsf W_\alpha, \qquad \langle\mathcal G_*^{[j]}\rangle_\theta\in \mathsf M_\mu. The mean coefficients extend smoothly by zero outside the active shell. The next pulse inverse is applied exactly to the coefficients fγ,m[j]f_{\gamma,m}^{[j]} in (9.4).

    Wab[j]=⟨wa[j]wb[j]⟩θ,𝒫[j]=∫⟨gr[j]⟩YdR,pm[j]=𝖳0(gr[j]−ρ𝒫[j]),⟨𝒢*[j]+ℱ*[j]−ℰB,*⟩θ=(Drpm[j]−gr[j],Eθ[j],Ez[j]),\begin{equation} \begin{gathered} W_{ab}^{[j]}=\langle w_a^{[j]}w_b^{[j]}\rangle_\theta, \qquad \mathcal P^{[j]}=\int\langle g_r^{[j]}\rangle_Y\,dR, \qquad p_m^{[j]}=\mathsf T_0(g_r^{[j]}-\rho\mathcal P^{[j]}),\\ \langle\mathcal G_*^{[j]}+\mathcal F_*^{[j]}-\mathcal E_{B,*}\rangle_\theta =\bigl(D_r p_m^{[j]}-g_r^{[j]},E_\theta^{[j]},E_z^{[j]}\bigr), \end{gathered} \tag{9.6} \end{equation}(9.6) Here gr[j],Eθ[j],Ez[j]g_r^{[j]},E_\theta^{[j]},E_z^{[j]} are the values given by (8.3) for this tuple.

Proof.

First prove (i). Then keep track of the additive errors in (ii) while preserving the exact mean equations in (iii).

Part (i), support and coefficient bounds. The primary pulses have the stated supports and weighted bounds at every derivative order. Differentiation preserves both the closed support and the amplitude-class bounds. Each explicit DrD_r costs κs\kappa_s. Taking more amplitude derivatives of that estimate can make its constants and polynomial degrees larger, but it does not charge that exponent loss a second time.

In a product of a mean and a wave, the product keeps the wave’s slow support, transverse support, local torus rectangle, and PvP_v factor. Multiplying two waves with one label adds their integer phase multipliers. Their zero harmonic is exactly their angular mean, because the angular frequency kpkp is a nonzero integer. Every other output keeps the wave weight, since Pv2≤PvP_v^2\le P_v. Different labels do not interact. Taking curls, forming pressure coefficients, and propagating a particular pulse all preserve the phase integer. Mean operations cannot create a nonzero angular harmonic. Any nonzero harmonic produced later still contains a wave factor, so it keeps that factor’s support and envelope.

The radial integration, pressure reconstruction, mean-vector-potential construction, and auxiliary-time inversion from Section 8 all preserve the bounds for mean amplitudes. For the stress correction in Proposition 7.6, subtract a supported interior profile with the same weighted radial moment as the source. The corrected source then has total moment zero. Its weighted radial integral can therefore be taken forward from the left edge of its support or backward from the right edge. Near either edge, let ss be the matching logarithmic distance from (6.23). There, the weight ζ\zeta is e−a/s2e^{-a/s^2} times a smooth positive factor with fixed positive upper and lower bounds, where a>0a>0 is fixed. For every fixed M≥0M\ge 0 and every integer k≥0k\ge 0, sufficiently small positive δ,s\delta,s satisfy

∫0δs−Me−a/s2ds≤CM,aδ3−Me−a/δ2,|dkdske−a/s2|≤Ck,as−3ke−a/s2.\int_0^\delta s^{-M}e^{-a/s^2}\,ds \le C_{M,a}\delta^{3-M}e^{-a/\delta^2}, \qquad \left|\frac{d^k}{ds^k}e^{-a/s^2}\right| \le C_{k,a}s^{-3k}e^{-a/s^2}. The substitution v=a/s2v=a/s^2 gives the first bound, and direct differentiation gives the second. On the normalized shell, the radial weights and the radial Jacobian are bounded. Differentiating the radial integral therefore leaves a bound of the form ζδ−M′\zeta\delta^{-M'}, where M′M' can depend on the derivative. In the interior, ζ\zeta has a positive lower bound. A source of order α\alpha therefore gives a stress correction Σ∈𝖬α\Sigma\in \mathsf M_\alpha.

For the amplitude division, use the same normalization as in (7.31), namely dΣ=𝖧−1(Σ/ε)d_\Sigma=\mathsf H^{-1}(\Sigma/\varepsilon) and δaσ=(dΣ)σ/(2aσ)\delta a_\sigma=(d_\Sigma)_\sigma/(2a_\sigma). The inverse-matrix bounds and (7.25) give the following estimates for every fixed coefficient multi-index II.

|DI(dΣ)σ|≤CIεα−1S*bIζδ−MI,|DI(aσ−1)|≤CIS*bIζ−1/2δ−MI,|DIδaσ|≤CIεα−1S*bI′ζδ−MI′,|DI(εδaσbσ)|≤CIεα−1/2S*bI″ζδ−MI″Pv.\begin{aligned} |D^I(d_\Sigma)_\sigma| &\le C_I\varepsilon^{\alpha-1}S_*^{b_I}\zeta\delta^{-M_I},\\ |D^I(a_\sigma^{-1})| &\le C_I S_*^{b_I}\zeta^{-1/2}\delta^{-M_I},\\ |D^I\delta a_\sigma| &\le C_I\varepsilon^{\alpha-1}S_*^{b'_I}\sqrt\zeta\,\delta^{-M'_I},\\ |D^I(\sqrt\varepsilon\,\delta a_\sigma b_\sigma)| &\le C_I\varepsilon^{\alpha-1/2}S_*^{b''_I}\sqrt\zeta\,\delta^{-M''_I}P_v. \end{aligned} This gives (7.33) again. The last line also uses the fundamental pulse bounds. After the slow cutoff, it is the 𝖶α−1/2\mathsf W_{\alpha-1/2} estimate from Proposition 7.6. The remaining square-root weight at the edge makes the extension by zero smooth.

Each new source now satisfies the assumptions of Proposition 7.2. Along its prescribed path, the slow and transverse variables are fixed. If the data are zero all along one of these paths, the solution is zero there as well. The final cutoff puts the support back inside the fixed enlarged local torus rectangle. A source with a smooth extension gives a solution with a smooth extension. This proves the support condition needed by the inverse. There is no need to divide by the original cutoff.

The set of local bands stays fixed. Radial paths keep (z,t)(z,t) fixed, and qq depends only on (z,t)(z,t). Temporal inversion and pulse propagation keep all slow variables fixed. The common-torus construction from Lemma 6.2 therefore applies at every step of the finite construction. A radial mean can collect a number of labels that grows polynomially in S*S_*, while only a bounded number of wave labels overlap at any one point. This radial collection changes only the polynomial factors in S*S_*. It does not change the common chart or the ε\varepsilon exponent.

Parts (ii) and (iii), flat errors and exact means. When an actual increment is (w,π)(w,\pi), the residual changes by

ℛ(u+w,p+π)=ℛ(u,p)+∂tw−Δw+∇π+(u⋅∇)w+(w⋅∇)u+(w⋅∇)w.\begin{aligned} \mathscr R(u+w,p+\pi)={}&\mathscr R(u,p)+\partial_t w-\Delta w+\nabla\pi\\ &+(u\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla)w+(w\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla)u+(w\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla)w. \end{aligned} The old ℱ\mathcal F is added directly. Every product in the display uses the actual fields, including the curls with their cutoffs and the remainders from the modified radial integral with compact support. Put every newly created flat term into ℱ\mathcal F. At any fixed stage, there are only finitely many kinds of these terms. The Gaussian bound in Proposition 9.1 is uniform over the labels. Lemma 8.2 bounds each cutoff remainder by any chosen power of qq, at the cost of using finitely many more source derivatives. Summing a number of labels that grows polynomially does not spoil those bounds. Keep the Gaussian cutoff tails with nonzero harmonics in the additive residual, and do not feed them into later forward pulse solves. The mean residuals Eθ,EzE_\theta,E_z are the exact conservative balances and may contain flat cutoff remainders, which a fixed mean inverse may cancel. If a contribution is canceled, remove it from ℱ\mathcal F. The cutoff-remainder estimates put the remainder in 𝖬α\mathsf M_\alpha for every α\alpha. This update keeps both the stated classes and the exact splitting of the residual. It proves (9.5) at every finite stage, which proves (ii). Apply Proposition 8.1 to the full current tuple and use (8.12). This gives (9.6) and proves (iii). ◻

In the realization step, the finite corrections are summed to build the infinite local field. Its residual is controlled by comparing that field with one fixed finite stage. The flat residuals from the separate stages are not added together.

9.3 Starting the iteration and running a full correction cycle

The primary pulses, followed by the first mean corrections, give the first residual bounds in Proposition 9.5. Proposition 9.6 then shows that a full cycle improves every one of those bounds while keeping the support and moment conditions. The induction statement below combines the residual orders in (9.8) with the bounds on the total velocity correction in (9.9). Those total bounds control how the existing correction interacts with every later increment.

Throughout the construction, keep the base (b,V,G)(b,V,G), the primary amplitudes, and every inverse operator fixed. Let w0tan=W0asw_0^{\mathrm{tan}}=W_0^{\mathrm{as}} be the normalized representative of the assembled primary transverse field from (7.35). For each finite construction, write its normalized velocity and pressure as

u*=(b+β,V+v,G+γ)+w,p*=pB,*+pm+pw,⟨w⟩θ=⟨pw⟩θ=0.\begin{equation} u_*=(b+\beta,V+v,G+\gamma)+w, \qquad p_*=p_{B,*}+p_m+p_w, \qquad \langle w\rangle_\theta=\langle p_w\rangle_\theta=0. \tag{9.7} \end{equation}(9.7) Here pB,*p_{B,*} is the pressure of the base, pwp_w is the sum of the pressure harmonics supplied by the amplitude equations, and pmp_m is reconstructed from the current grg_r through (8.12). Equations (8.3), (8.12), and (8.15) then determine Eθ,Ez,𝒫,𝒥θ,𝒥zE_\theta,E_z,\mathcal P,\mathcal J_\theta,\mathcal J_z.

Definition 9.4 (Finite correction state).

For j∈ℕ∪{0}j\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}, a state at stage jj consists of real fields of the form (9.7) with the properties listed next. The wave ww is a sum of curls of supported wave potentials with the fixed phases for each label. The mean correction (β,v,γ)(\beta,v,\gamma) is the sum of the curl of an azimuthal potential and an azimuthal field added directly. Both velocity corrections are therefore exactly divergence-free. The source supports, finite sets of harmonics, smooth extensions by zero, and physical residual splitting are the ones in Proposition 9.3.

9.4 One common domain and estimates for physical derivatives.

To use Lemma 5.4, every finite state (u[j],p[j])(u^{[j]},p^{[j]}) must exist on the same domain. Lemma 9.7 provides that domain. The gain in decay must also survive differentiation in the physical variables. More exactly, once the derivative order is fixed, the loss in powers of qq must not depend on the correction stage. The constants in the bounds may still depend on that stage, as Lemma 9.8 allows.

Lemma 9.7.

There is a number qbig>0q_{\mathrm{big}}>0 that does not depend on the correction stage or the derivative order, and every finite partial sum above, before its summation cutoffs are applied, is defined on 0<q<qbig0<q<q_{\mathrm{big}}. Once the stage and the order of an output amplitude derivative are fixed, constructing and estimating that derivative needs only finitely many derivatives of the input amplitudes. The constants may depend on the correction stage.

Proof.

Choose 0<qbig≤q*0<q_{\mathrm{big}}\le q_* once and for all so that the pulse estimates hold whenever q<qbigq<q_{\mathrm{big}}. Make this choice with the fixed background, the stated positive lower bound for |nΦ||n_\Phi|, the primary covariance, and the fixed supports of the normalized mean-correction profiles. Every later inhomogeneous amplitude problem is a linear equation whose coefficients are these fixed ones and whose source is already known. The same threshold works for every harmonic because (7.18) writes its propagator as the fundamental propagator times a forward damping factor whose magnitude is at most one. At each fixed derivative order, differentiation puts powers of the harmonic integer into the constants and allows polynomial growth in S*S_*. It does not call for a smaller qq-threshold, as Corollary 7.3 shows.

The signed updates divide by the original 2yσ2\sqrt{y_\sigma} in (7.31), and the finite-dimensional correction system uses the fixed linear map from Lemma 8.7. Pressure, the temporal inverses, and the modified radial integrals that define the mean potentials are all fixed linear maps. The primary construction fixes every inverse coefficient and every denominator. These finite operations are therefore defined on the same domain for sources of any size, including sources near qbigq_{\mathrm{big}}. Each cycle improves the decay exponent on that whole domain.

The number of input derivatives needed at a given stage can be counted with a directed acyclic graph. Each vertex is an intermediate expression, and each arrow records one of the sums, products, derivatives, or proved inverses used to build a later expression from an earlier one. Directed means that these arrows point from input toward output. Acyclic means that no chain of arrows loops back to where it started. The source vertices, where no earlier expression feeds in, are the input fields. For a source vertex aa, let Dv,a(m)D_{v,a}(m) be any sufficient number of derivatives of the input aa for bounding, through derivative order mm, the expression at vertex vv. Differentiating a pulse equation to order mm gives an equation containing amplitude derivatives of order at most mm; the lower-order derivatives are already controlled. The torus inverses need finitely many more amplitude derivatives, while the modified radial integrals keep the stated derivative bounds. To make the cutoff remainder flat to a chosen power, integrate the same exact integral by parts only finitely many times. These counts tell exactly how many source derivatives need estimates. The finite partial sums (u[j],p[j])(u^{[j]},p^{[j]}) now have residuals whose decay can be made arbitrarily high on one common domain. 10 A compactly supported force and breakdown on all of space

This section turns the fields from Theorem 3.1 into the solution and force on all of space in Theorem 1.1. Write the local fields as

uloc=curl⁡𝒜+ℬeθ,ploc.u^{\mathrm{loc}}=\operatorname{curl}\mathcal A+\mathcal Be_\theta, \qquad p^{\mathrm{loc}}. Here 𝒜\mathcal A and ℬ\mathcal B are the representatives built in (9.21), and ℬ\mathcal B does not depend on θ\theta. Start with viscosity one. The local velocity has the growth in (3.6) required by Theorem 1.1. What remains is to give it zero initial data and compact spatial support while making its momentum residual agree, before time one, with a force in Cc∞(ℝ3×(0,∞);ℝ3)C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times(0,\infty);\mathbb R^3). This is done in Proposition 10.1 and Lemma 10.3.

Multiply the vector potential, the azimuthal coefficient, and the pressure by cutoffs that equal one near (0,1)(0,1). Lemma 10.2 then proves that every derivative of the new residual has a uniform limit as t↑1t\uparrow 1, and Lemma 10.3 builds a force for t>1t>1 whose derivatives attain all those limits. Before time one, the equation gives a uniform energy bound in Lemma 10.4. Lemma 10.5 then compares this field with any smooth solution of bounded kinetic energy. That comparison transfers the growth of the local velocity to the smooth solution and gives the contradiction needed for Theorem 1.1. Rescaling gives every positive viscosity and also gives the periodic construction in Corollary 10.6.

10.1 Keeping the construction inside the local domain.

This subsection places the velocity and pressure inside the domain from Theorem 3.1. First recall why the chosen vector potential 𝒜\mathcal A is smooth at the axis, as stated in Theorem 3.1(i), and why it vanishes in the heat exterior from (3.5). Because of these two facts, its curl can be taken after the localization, and the force at time one can be estimated in Lemma 10.2. For the background coefficients UnU_n from (5.1), the Stokes streamfunctions and their sum are

Equations (4.28) and (5.10) give ∫0∞Un(X,η)dX=0\int_0^\infty U_n(X,\eta)\,dX=0 for every n≥0n\geq 0. Each radial integral in (10.1) is therefore zero beyond the common support of the axial coefficients. Near the axis, 𝒮=r2a(r2,z,t)\mathcal S=r^2a(r^2,z,t) for a smooth scalar aa, so

Their supports satisfy supp⁡u(⋅,t)∪supp⁡p(⋅,t)⊂𝒦\operatorname{supp}u(\mathord\cdot,t)\cup\operatorname{supp}p(\mathord\cdot,t)\subset\mathcal K for every 0≤t<10\leq t<1, and they also satisfy

div⁡u=0,u(⋅,t)=p(⋅,t)=0for all sufficiently small t≥0.\begin{equation} \operatorname{div}u=0, \qquad u(\mathord\cdot,t)=p(\mathord\cdot,t)=0 \qquad\text{for all sufficiently small }t\geq0. \tag{10.2} \end{equation}(10.2) These fields agree with uloc,plocu^{\mathrm{loc}},p^{\mathrm{loc}} on a spatial neighborhood of the origin for every time sufficiently close to 11.

For 0≤t<10\leq t<1, define

f=ℛ(u,p)=∂tu+(u⋅∇)u−Δu+∇p.\begin{equation} f=\mathscr R(u,p)=\partial_tu+(u\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla)u-\Delta u+\nabla p. \tag{10.5} \end{equation}(10.5) This definition includes every derivative of the cutoffs. Taking its divergence gives

−Δp=∑i,j=13∂i∂j(uiuj)−div⁡f.-\Delta p=\sum_{i,j=1}^3\partial_i\partial_j(u_iu_j)-\operatorname{div}f. The localized pressure therefore satisfies the Poisson equation with the matching term from the divergence of the force. The force is allowed to have nonzero divergence.

10.2 Limits of force derivatives at the final time.

So far, the force in (10.5) is defined only for t<1t<1. To extend it smoothly past time one, all of its derivatives must have compatible limits as t↑1t\uparrow 1. At the origin, those limits are controlled by the flatness of the local residual in (3.4). Away from the origin, the terms introduced by localization are controlled by the endpoint bounds in Theorem 3.1(ii) and the exact exterior heat flow in (3.5). Lemma 10.2 first proves the derivative limits. Lemma 10.3 then builds an extension with compact support in time.

Lemma 10.2.

For every spatial multi-index α\alpha and every integer j≥0j\geq 0, the derivative ∂xα∂tjf\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^jf converges uniformly on ℝ3\mathbb R^3 as t↑1t\uparrow 1. There are functions Fj∈Cc∞(ℝ3;ℝ3)F_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3), all supported in 𝒦\mathcal K, such that

limt↑1∂xα∂tjf(x,t)=∂xαFj(x),∂xαFj(0)=0.\begin{equation} \lim_{t\uparrow1}\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^jf(x,t)=\partial_x^\alpha F_j(x), \qquad \partial_x^\alpha F_j(0)=0. \tag{10.6} \end{equation}(10.6) These are the derivative limits of ff from t<1t<1, and they agree with both spatial and time differentiation.

Proof.

Start with endpoint bounds away from the origin. Take a compact spatial set on which qq has a positive lower bound and stays away from q*q_*. Theorem 3.1(ii) bounds every physical derivative of the actual potentials and scalar fields there. More exactly, let K0K_0 be such a compact set, let G=𝒜,ℬeθ,plocG=\mathcal A,\mathcal Be_\theta,p^{\mathrm{loc}}, and take t<t′<1t<t'<1. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives

supK0|∂xα∂tjG(⋅,t′)−∂xα∂tjG(⋅,t)|≤|t′−t|supK0×[t,t′]|∂xα∂tj+1G|.\sup_{K_0}|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^jG(\mathord\cdot,t') -\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^jG(\mathord\cdot,t)| \leq|t'-t|\sup_{K_0\times[t,t']}|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^{j+1}G|. The last supremum has a bound near time one that does not depend on t,t′t,t'. Every fixed derivative is therefore uniformly Cauchy as t↑1t\uparrow 1. These constants may depend on the chosen positive lower bound for qq.

The argument in Proposition 9.9 that leaves only finitely many nonzero cutoff terms gives these bounds on the closed parameter range −1≤η≤1-1\leq\eta\leq 1. It gives them for the actual representatives and for the smooth Cartesian factors in their near-axis forms, while the labels and integer frequencies stay fixed. Multiplying by the fixed cutoffs and applying the finite differential expression (10.5) keep the bounds.

In the region that remains, rr has a positive lower bound and qq is small enough that X≥XextX\geq X_{\mathrm{ext}}. The velocity there is the exterior azimuthal field K(r,τ)eθK(r,\tau)e_\theta from (3.5). In terms of the heat profile ℋ\mathcal H defined in (A.32),

K(r,τ)=c∞s−Aℋ(2τ/s),s=r2/2.\begin{equation} K(r,\tau)=c_\infty s^{-A}\mathcal H(2\tau/s), \qquad s=r^2/2. \tag{10.7} \end{equation}(10.7) Thus the function in Theorem 3.1 is ℋext(Z)=2Ac∞ℋ(4Z)\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ext}}(Z)=2^Ac_\infty\mathcal H(4Z). For each jj, the integral in (A.32) can be differentiated uniformly for Z≥0Z\geq 0 because its differentiated integrand is bounded by a constant times e−vvh+je^{-v}v^{h+j}. It follows that

|∂τjK(r,τ)|≤Cjr−1−2h−2j,|∂τjK(ρ,τ)2ρ|≤Cjρ−3−4h−2j.\begin{equation} |\partial_\tau^jK(r,\tau)|\leq C_jr^{-1-2h-2j}, \qquad \left|\partial_\tau^j\frac{K(\rho,\tau)^2}{\rho}\right| \leq C_j\rho^{-3-4h-2j}. \tag{10.8} \end{equation}(10.8) The pressure is normalized to vanish at radial infinity. On a compact interval of positive radii r∈[r−,r+]r\in[r_-,r_+], where r−>0r_->0, the second upper bound is integrable over ρ≥r−\rho\geq r_-. Dominated convergence therefore gives

∂τjploc(r,τ)=−∫r∞∂τj(K(ρ,τ)2ρ)dρ.\partial_\tau^jp^{\mathrm{loc}}(r,\tau) =-\int_r^\infty\partial_\tau^j\left(\frac{K(\rho,\tau)^2}{\rho}\right)\,d\rho. It also gives a uniform bound and a one-sided limit for every derivative on each compact interval of positive radii. Here ∂t=−∂τ\partial_t=-\partial_\tau. Differentiate the lower endpoint to get the higher radial derivatives of the pressure, and differentiate (10.7) directly to get those of KK. This gives the required smooth one-sided extension to τ=0\tau=0, using the integral on τ≥0\tau\geq 0. In this region 𝒜=0\mathcal A=0, so after localization the fields contain only these smooth exterior quantities and the fixed cutoffs. The heat equation for KK and the identity ∂rploc=K2/r\partial_rp^{\mathrm{loc}}=K^2/r also show directly that the residual of the uncut exterior field is exactly zero.

These two regions cover the final time slice away from the origin. If z≠0z\neq 0, then q≥|z|1/D>0q\geq|z|^{1/D}>0. If z=0z=0 and x≠0x\neq 0, then r>0r>0, and the exterior argument above applies on a small neighborhood. Every Cartesian space–time derivative of the force therefore converges uniformly on compact spatial sets that do not contain the origin.

Near the origin, both cutoffs equal one. Use (3.4) on X≤XextX\leq X_{\mathrm{ext}}, and use the exactly zero residual when XX is larger. For every α,j,N\alpha,j,N, this gives, on one fixed neighborhood of (0,1)(0,1),

|∂xα∂tjf(x,t)|≤Cα,j,N(τ+|z|1/D)N.\begin{equation} |\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^jf(x,t)| \leq C_{\alpha,j,N}\bigl(\tau+|z|^{1/D}\bigr)^N. \tag{10.9} \end{equation}(10.9) Given any tolerance, first choose a small ball and then choose a time close enough to one that this bound is below the tolerance throughout the ball. A finite cover of the part of 𝒦\mathcal K outside that ball gives uniform convergence there. Every one of these derivatives is zero outside 𝒦\mathcal K. They are therefore uniformly Cauchy on ℝ3\mathbb R^3, and their limits are zero at the origin.

Define FjF_j as the uniform limit for α=0\alpha=0. Pass to the limit in the fundamental theorem of calculus along segments parallel to the spatial coordinate axes. This identifies every other limit as ∂xαFj\partial_x^\alpha F_j. It follows that FjF_j is smooth and has the stated support. Passing to the limit in the matching identity in time gives

∂xα∂tjf(x,t)=∂xαFj(x)−∫t1∂xα∂tj+1f(x,s)ds.\begin{equation} \partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^jf(x,t) =\partial_x^\alpha F_j(x)-\int_t^1\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^{j+1}f(x,s)\,ds. \tag{10.10} \end{equation}(10.10) This proves that the derivative limits agree with both spatial and time differentiation, and it finishes the proof of (10.6). ◻

The limits FjF_j are the Taylor coefficients needed to continue the force through time one. Give the coefficients time cutoffs whose supports shrink as the derivative order grows, so the extension also has compact support in time. A smooth force with compact support has the decay required in [13, (5)], and the zero initial data has the required initial-data properties as well.

Lemma 10.3.

The force in (10.5) extends to f∈Cc∞(ℝ3×(0,∞);ℝ3)f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times(0,\infty);\mathbb R^3), with support in 𝒦×[0,2]\mathcal K\times[0,2].

Proof.

Choose χ0∈Cc∞(ℝ)\chi_0\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R) so that it equals one near zero and equals zero whenever its argument is at least one. For σ=t−1≥0\sigma=t-1\geq 0, set

On the support of each summand, 0≤σ≤bj−10\leq\sigma\leq b_j^{-1}. The product rule then gives

∥∂xα∂σm(χ0(bjσ)σjj!Fj)∥∞≤Cj,mbjm−j∥Fj∥C|α|.\begin{equation} \left\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\sigma^m \left(\chi_0(b_j\sigma)\frac{\sigma^j}{j!}F_j\right)\right\|_\infty \leq C_{j,m}b_j^{m-j}\|F_j\|_{C^{|\alpha|}}. \tag{10.12} \end{equation}(10.12) To see this, suppose aa derivatives land on the cutoff. Their factor bjab_j^a is multiplied by a monomial of degree j−m+aj-m+a, which is bounded by bj−(j−m+a)b_j^{-(j-m+a)}. If that monomial has been differentiated to zero, the term is absent. Set b0=1b_0=1. For j≥1j\geq 1, define

bj=min⁡{b∈ℕ:b>bj−1,maxa,m≥0a+m≤⌊j/2⌋Cj,mbm−j∥Fj∥Ca≤2−j},b_j=\min\left\{b\in\mathbb N:b>b_{j-1},\quad \max_{\substack{a,m\geq0\\a+m\leq\lfloor j/2\rfloor}} C_{j,m}b^{m-j}\|F_j\|_{C^a}\leq2^{-j}\right\}, where the maximum is taken over nonnegative integers a,ma,m. This gives only finitely many conditions, and each one has m−j<0m-j<0. So the defining set contains at least one integer. With this choice, (10.12) is at most 2−j2^{-j} whenever |α|+m≤⌊j/2⌋|\alpha|+m\leq\lfloor j/2\rfloor.

After any fixed number of derivatives, the tail now converges uniformly. At σ=0\sigma=0, the cutoff in each fixed summand is constant on a neighborhood of zero. Its mm-th derivative therefore contributes only when j=mj=m, and that contribution is FmF_m. Uniform convergence after differentiation, together with (10.10), shows that (10.11) matches every mixed space–time derivative limit from t<1t<1. Every summand keeps its support in 𝒦\mathcal K and is zero when σ≥1\sigma\geq 1. The same uniform convergence proves smoothness at those support boundaries. For the decay bounds, choose RR with 𝒦⊂B(0,R)\mathcal K\subset B(0,R), and write Mα,m=∥∂xα∂tmf∥∞M_{\alpha,m}=\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^mf\|_\infty. Since the force has compact support, every integer k≥0k\geq 0 satisfies

|∂xα∂tmf(x,t)|≤Mα,m(3+R)k(1+|x|+t)−k.|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^mf(x,t)| \leq M_{\alpha,m}(3+R)^k(1+|x|+t)^{-k}. ◻

10.3 Energy and comparison.

This subsection starts by proving that the smooth compactly supported force ff from Lemma 10.3 gives an energy bound for the constructed velocity uu that stays uniform up to time one (Lemma 10.4). Next it proves that any smooth solution with the same force, zero initial data, and bounded kinetic energy must agree with that velocity on every shorter time interval (Lemma 10.5). This comparison lets the proof carry the local velocity growth in (3.6) over to any supposed global smooth solution. In these energy estimates on all of space, ∥⋅∥p\|\cdot\|_p is the spatial Lp(ℝ3)L^p(\mathbb{R}^3) norm, and every spatial integral with no domain written beside it is over ℝ3\mathbb{R}^3.

Lemma 10.4.

Set ℱ(t)=∫0t∥f(s)∥2ds\mathcal F(t)=\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_2\,ds for 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1. Then ℱ(1)<∞\mathcal F(1)<\infty, and ∥u(t)∥22+2∫0t∥∇u(s)∥22ds≤ℱ(t)2(0≤t<1).\begin{equation} \|u(t)\|_2^2+2\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_2^2\,ds \leq \mathcal F(t)^2 \qquad (0\leq t<1). \tag{10.13} \end{equation}(10.13) In particular, the kinetic energy stays uniformly bounded, and the total dissipation on [0,1)[0,1) is finite.

Proof.

On any interval [0,T][0,T] with T<1T<1, the localized velocity and pressure are smooth and have support in one fixed compact spatial set. Taking the inner product of the equation with uu and integrating in space gives 12ddt∥u(t)∥22+∥∇u(t)∥22=⟨f(t),u(t)⟩.\begin{equation} \frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|u(t)\|_2^2+\|\nabla u(t)\|_2^2 =\langle f(t),u(t)\rangle. \tag{10.14} \end{equation}(10.14) For δ>0\delta>0, divide this identity by (∥u(t)∥22+δ2)1/2(\|u(t)\|_2^2+\delta^2)^{1/2}, drop the nonnegative dissipation term, and apply Cauchy–Schwarz. Integrate from the zero initial data and then let δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0. The result is ∥u(t)∥2≤ℱ(t)\|u(t)\|_2\leq\mathcal F(t). Put this bound back into (10.14) and integrate once more to get ∥u(t)∥22+2∫0t∥∇u(s)∥22ds≤2∫0tℱ′(s)ℱ(s)ds=ℱ(t)2.\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_2^2\,ds \leq 2\int_0^t\mathcal F'(s)\mathcal F(s)\,ds =\mathcal F(t)^2. Because the force is smooth and compactly supported, ℱ(1)<∞\mathcal F(1)<\infty. Monotone convergence then shows that the integrated dissipation on [0,1)[0,1) is finite, using only the bounds already proved for t<1t<1. ◻

The comparison argument only needs smoothness and a uniform spatial L2L^2 bound on [0,T][0,T], where T<1T<1. These assumptions put no restriction on how the spatial derivatives grow at infinity. The equation will first be used to find the pressure gradient, and only then will the proof take the limit in the localized energy identity.

Lemma 10.5.

Fix T<1T<1. Suppose v,Pv,P is a smooth solution of (1.1) with viscosity one on ℝ3×[0,T]\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,T]. Suppose it has the force ff from Lemma 10.3, zero initial velocity, and v∈L∞([0,T];L2(ℝ3))v\in L^\infty([0,T];L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)). Then v=uv=u on that whole interval, where uu is the localized velocity from Proposition 10.1.

Proof.

Take the difference of the two solutions and estimate it on balls whose radii grow without bound. The pressure term needs its own estimate because nothing has been assumed about the spatial growth of PP. Each constant written as CTC_T below may depend on TT and on the stated bounds for the fields, but it does not depend on the cutoff radius. Set w=v−u,π=P−p,gij=vivj−uiuj=wiwj+wiuj+uiwj.w=v-u,\qquad \pi=P-p,\qquad g_{ij}=v_iv_j-u_iu_j=w_iw_j+w_iu_j+u_iw_j. The convention is (div⁡g)i=∑j∂jgij(\operatorname{div}g)_i=\sum_j\partial_jg_{ij}. On [0,T][0,T], ∥w(t)∥2≤CT\|w(t)\|_2\leq C_T and ∑i,j∥gij(t)∥1≤CT\sum_{i,j}\|g_{ij}(t)\|_1\leq C_T. The same force appears in both equations, so it cancels and leaves ∂tw+(v⋅∇)w+(w⋅∇)u=Δw−∇π,div⁡w=0.\begin{equation} \partial_t w+(v\cdot\nabla)w+(w\cdot\nabla)u =\Delta w-\nabla\pi,\qquad \operatorname{div}w=0. \tag{10.15} \end{equation}(10.15)

10.3.0.1 Pressure gradient.

Let RiR_i be the Riesz transform whose Fourier multiplier is iξi/|ξ|i\xi_i/|\xi|, and define the pressure as a distribution, a continuous linear rule that assigns a number to each smooth compactly supported test function, by π*=∑i,j=13RiRjgij.\begin{equation} \pi_*=\sum_{i,j=1}^3 R_iR_jg_{ij}. \tag{10.16} \end{equation}(10.16)

The multiplier for this operator is −ξiξj/|ξ|2-\xi_i\xi_j/|\xi|^2; its value at zero does not matter. The Fourier transform of an L1L^1 function is bounded, so π*\pi_* is uniformly in H−s(ℝ3)H^{-s}(\mathbb{R}^3) for every s>3/2s>3/2. More exactly, its squared norm is at most a constant times ∥g∥12∫ℝ3(1+|ξ|2)−sdξ\|g\|_1^2\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}(1+|\xi|^2)^{-s}\,d\xi. The multiplier also gives Δπ*=−∑i,j∂i∂jgij.\Delta\pi_*=-\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_jg_{ij}. The next step is to prove that ∇π=∇π*\nabla\pi=\nabla\pi_* in the space–time interior. Take a∈Cc∞(0,T)a\in C_c^\infty(0,T). Writing (10.15) in conservative form gives ∫0Ta∇πdt=Δ∫0Tawdt+∫0Ta′wdt−div⁡∫0Tagdt.\int_0^T a\nabla\pi\,dt =\Delta\int_0^T aw\,dt+\int_0^T a'w\,dt -\operatorname{div}\int_0^T ag\,dt. The three terms on the right belong, in that order, to H−2H^{-2}, L2L^2, and H−3H^{-3}. The last one has this property because g∈Lt∞Lx1g\in L_t^\infty L_x^1, and the Fourier estimate above can be used with s=2s=2. Also, π*∈Lt∞Hx−2\pi_*\in L_t^\infty H_x^{-2}, so Ha:=∫0Ta(∇π−∇π*)dt∈H−3(ℝ3).H_a:=\int_0^T a(\nabla\pi-\nabla\pi_*)\,dt\in H^{-3}(\mathbb{R}^3). Taking the divergence of the difference equation gives Δπ=−∑i,j∂i∂jgij=Δπ*\Delta\pi=-\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_jg_{ij}=\Delta\pi_*. It follows that ΔHa=0\Delta H_a=0. The Fourier transform of HaH_a is a weighted L2L^2 function supported at the single point {0}\{0\}, so it must be zero. Allowing a spatial test function as well proves the stated equality. The equation has now determined the pressure gradient under these assumptions without putting any restriction on the spatial growth of PP.

10.3.0.2 Pressure flux.

Next, bound the pressure contribution on the boundary of an expanding ball by the weighted dissipation inside that ball. Start with ∫πw⋅∇χR\int\pi w\cdot\nabla\chi_R. 10.4 Growth, lifespan, and viscosity.

The force extension and energy estimate for the localized fields (u,p)(u,p) are now in place (Lemma 10.3, (10.13)). This subsection uses the inner growth asymptotic (3.6) from Theorem 3.1 to find the maximal classical lifespan. Together with the comparison lemma, Lemma 10.5, the same formula rules out a global smooth solution with bounded energy. A spatial rescaling then gives the result for every fixed positive viscosity without changing the time of the singularity.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

By (10.5), the field constructed above solves the equation exactly on [0,1)[0,1). Its smoothness and fixed compact support give u∈C([0,T];H3)u\in C([0,T];H^3) for every T<1T<1. Lemma 10.3 gives the force the required smoothness and support, and Lemma 10.4 gives the bounded energy.

Fix the XinX_{\mathrm{in}} from Theorem 3.1, and take the Cartesian points xτ=(2Xinτ,0,0),t=1−τ.\begin{equation} x_\tau=(\sqrt2X_{\mathrm{in}}\tau,0,0),\qquad t=1-\tau. \tag{10.20} \end{equation}(10.20) Along this path, z=0z=0 and q=τq=\tau. For every sufficiently small τ>0\tau>0, the spatial and time cutoffs in (10.4) both equal one. Equation (3.6) then gives uθ(xτ,1−τ)=τ−A(e0+O(τ2h))→+∞.\begin{equation} u_\theta(x_\tau,1-\tau) =\tau^{-A}\bigl(e_0+O(\tau^{2h})\bigr)\longrightarrow+\infty. \tag{10.21} \end{equation}(10.21) The annular corrections vanish in this fixed inner similarity region. In the expansion, the cutoff sum of the terms with n≥1n\geq 1, in powers of q2hq^{2h}, has exactly the relative-error bound shown here, with the summation cutoffs still included. The points xτx_\tau where the velocity diverges approach the origin. Since H3(ℝ3)↪L∞(ℝ3)H^3(\mathbb{R}^3)\hookrightarrow L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3), there can be no classical H3H^3 continuation through time one. In the classical H3H^3 class, Sobolev approximation justifies the same difference energy calculation, and H3↪W1,∞H^3\hookrightarrow W^{1,\infty} supplies the bound needed for Gronwall’s inequality. This proves uniqueness on every shorter interval. The maximal classical existence interval is therefore [0,1)[0,1).

Now suppose there were a global smooth solution v,Pv,P with the same data and uniformly bounded kinetic energy. For every T<1T<1, Lemma 10.5 applies on the closed interval [0,T][0,T], so v=uv=u throughout [0,1)[0,1). Equation (10.21) would then contradict the boundedness of the smooth field vv on a compact neighborhood of (0,1)(0,1). The force cannot be zero, because if it were, (10.13) would give u=0u=0.

Finally, fix ν>0\nu>0 and define uν(x,t)=νu(x/ν,t),pν(x,t)=νp(x/ν,t),fν(x,t)=νf(x/ν,t).\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} u_\nu(x,t)&=\sqrt\nu\,u(x/\sqrt\nu,t),\\ p_\nu(x,t)&=\nu p(x/\sqrt\nu,t), &f_\nu(x,t)&=\sqrt\nu\,f(x/\sqrt\nu,t). \end{aligned} \tag{10.22} \end{equation}(10.22) Put y=x/νy=x/\sqrt\nu. The chain rule gives ∂tuν+(uν⋅∇x)uν−νΔxuν+∇xpν=ν[∂tu+(u⋅∇y)u−Δyu+∇yp](y,t)=fν(x,t),∇x⋅uν(x,t)=(∇y⋅u)(y,t)=0.\begin{aligned} \partial_tu_\nu+(u_\nu\cdot\nabla_x)u_\nu-\nu\Delta_xu_\nu+\nabla_xp_\nu &=\sqrt\nu\,[\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla_y)u-\Delta_yu+\nabla_yp](y,t) =f_\nu(x,t),\\ \nabla_x\cdot u_\nu(x,t)&=(\nabla_y\cdot u)(y,t)=0. \end{aligned} The initial data are still zero, and the common spatial support becomes 𝒦ν=ν𝒦\mathcal K_\nu=\sqrt\nu\mathcal K. Time has not been rescaled, and ∂xα∂tmfν(x,t)=ν(1−|α|)/2(∂yα∂tmf)(x/ν,t).\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^m f_\nu(x,t) =\nu^{(1-|\alpha|)/2} (\partial_y^\alpha\partial_t^m f)(x/\sqrt\nu,t). So the force is still smooth and compactly supported in 𝒦ν×[0,2]\mathcal K_\nu\times[0,2], and it satisfies every required decay bound for this fixed ν>0\nu>0. The energy and dissipation scale as ∥uν(t)∥22=ν5/2∥u(t)∥22,ν∫01∥∇uν∥22dt=ν5/2∫01∥∇u∥22dt.\begin{equation} \|u_\nu(t)\|_2^2=\nu^{5/2}\|u(t)\|_2^2,\qquad \nu\int_0^1\|\nabla u_\nu\|_2^2\,dt =\nu^{5/2}\int_0^1\|\nabla u\|_2^2\,dt. \tag{10.23} \end{equation}(10.23) The growth occurs at νxτ\sqrt\nu x_\tau, still at time one. 10.5 The periodic equations.

The velocity, pressure, and force all have support in one fixed compact set (Proposition 10.1 and Lemma 10.3), so the construction can also be made periodic. First, rescale the supports until they lie inside a fundamental cube. Then add all their integer translates. The translated supports do not overlap, so the momentum equation, including its nonlinear term, stays intact. The pressure becomes periodic too, as the erratum to the problem statement requires [13].

The periodic domain and the interior of its fundamental cube are 𝕋3=ℝ3/ℤ3,Q0=(−1/2,1/2)3.\mathbb{T}^3=\mathbb{R}^3/\mathbb{Z}^3,\qquad Q_0=(-1/2,1/2)^3. The next corollary proves the periodic breakdown alternative (D) in [13].

Corollary 10.6.

For every ν>0\nu>0, there is a smooth force on 𝕋3×[0,∞)\mathbb{T}^3\times[0,\infty) with compact support in time such that the solution (U,Pper)(U,P_{\mathrm{per}}) of the periodic Navier–Stokes equations, with viscosity ν\nu and zero initial velocity, is smooth on [0,1)[0,1) and satisfies limsupt↑1∥U(t)∥L∞(𝕋3)=∞.\limsup_{t\uparrow1}\|U(t)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^3)}=\infty. Before time one, its velocity and pressure are supported in a fixed compact subset of the interior of Q0Q_0. No global smooth periodic solution exists for the same initial data and force.

Proof.

Fix the viscosity ν\nu, and call the whole-space fields and force already constructed u,p,fu,p,f. Their common spatial support lies in 𝒦ν=ν𝒦\mathcal K_\nu=\sqrt\nu\mathcal K, just as in the viscosity rescaling (10.22). Choose λ>1\lambda>1 large enough that λ−1𝒦ν⋐Q0\lambda^{-1}\mathcal K_\nu\Subset Q_0, and set t0=1−λ−2t_0=1-\lambda^{-2}. For t≥t0t\geq t_0, define ũ(x,t)=λu(λx,λ2(t−t0)),p̃(x,t)=λ2p(λx,λ2(t−t0)),f̃(x,t)=λ3f(λx,λ2(t−t0)).\begin{aligned} \widetilde u(x,t)&=\lambda u(\lambda x,\lambda^2(t-t_0)),\\ \widetilde p(x,t)&=\lambda^2p(\lambda x,\lambda^2(t-t_0)),\\ \widetilde f(x,t)&=\lambda^3f(\lambda x,\lambda^2(t-t_0)). \end{aligned} Use the first two formulas only for t<1t<1, and use the force formula for every t≥t0t\geq t_0. Extend all three fields by zero when t<t0t<t_0. They are smooth across t=t0t=t_0 because the original fields and force vanish on an interval after their initial time. Every term in the momentum equation is λ3\lambda^3 times the corresponding original term, so the viscosity is still ν\nu. The original time one is reached exactly when λ2(t−t0)=1\lambda^2(t-t_0)=1, which is t=1t=1.

Define the periodic fields by U(x,t)=∑k∈ℤ3ũ(x+k,t),0≤t<1,Pper(x,t)=∑k∈ℤ3p̃(x+k,t),0≤t<1,Fper(x,t)=∑k∈ℤ3f̃(x+k,t),t≥0.\begin{aligned} U(x,t)&=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^3}\widetilde u(x+k,t),&&0\leq t<1,\\ P_{\mathrm{per}}(x,t)&=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^3}\widetilde p(x+k,t),&&0\leq t<1,\\ F_{\mathrm{per}}(x,t)&=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^3}\widetilde f(x+k,t),&&t\geq0. \end{aligned} Different translates have disjoint supports, with a positive gap between them. These sums are locally finite, so derivatives pass through them, and at most one translate is nonzero at any point. In particular, (U⋅∇)U(x,t)=∑k∈ℤ3(ũ(x+k,t)⋅∇)ũ(x+k,t).(U\cdot\nabla)U(x,t) =\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^3}(\widetilde u(x+k,t)\cdot\nabla)\widetilde u(x+k,t). The periodic velocity, pressure, and force therefore solve the equation exactly: ∂tU+(U⋅∇)U−νΔU+∇Pper=Fper,div⁡U=0,U(⋅,0)=0.\partial_tU+(U\cdot\nabla)U-\nu\Delta U+\nabla P_{\mathrm{per}} =F_{\mathrm{per}},\qquad \operatorname{div}U=0,\qquad U(\cdot,0)=0.

The force is smooth, and its time support lies in [t0,1+λ−2][t_0,1+\lambda^{-2}]. On the torus, this gives every decay estimate ∥∂xα∂tmFper(t)∥∞≤Cα,m,N(1+t)−N\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_t^mF_{\mathrm{per}}(t)\|_\infty \leq C_{\alpha,m,N}(1+t)^{-N}. For the path xτx_\tau from (10.20), the rescaled growth path is x̃τ=λ−1νxτ,t̃τ=1−λ−2τ.\widetilde x_\tau=\lambda^{-1}\sqrt\nu x_\tau,\qquad \widetilde t_\tau=1-\lambda^{-2}\tau. This path stays inside Q0Q_0 near (0,1)(0,1), where only the zeroth translate is nonzero. Equations (10.21) and (10.22) give Uθ(x̃τ,t̃τ)=λντ−A(e0+O(τ2h))→+∞.U_\theta(\widetilde x_\tau,\widetilde t_\tau) =\lambda\sqrt\nu\,\tau^{-A}\bigl(e_0+O(\tau^{2h})\bigr)\longrightarrow+\infty.

Finally, take any two smooth periodic solutions with the same force and initial data on an interval [0,T][0,T] with T<1T<1. Their difference ww satisfies 12ddt∥w∥L2(𝕋3)2+ν∥∇w∥L2(𝕋3)2≤∥∇U∥∞∥w∥L2(𝕋3)2.\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|w\|_{L^2(\mathbb{T}^3)}^2 +\nu\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(\mathbb{T}^3)}^2 \leq\|\nabla U\|_\infty\|w\|_{L^2(\mathbb{T}^3)}^2. Periodic integration makes both the transport term and the pressure term disappear. Gronwall’s inequality shows that the two solutions agree through TT. Any global smooth solution would therefore equal UU before time one, which is impossible because its velocity blows up at t=1t=1. ◻

A Matching radial moments and constructing the heat exterior

This appendix constructs the outer part of the leading profile (U,E,Π)(U,E,\Pi) from Theorem 4.6. Its pressure integral gives the datum Π0\Pi_0 for the regular axis problem (Lemma A.5). Its moment conditions, including (A.8), make the radially integrated leading residual stress 𝒯0\mathcal T_0 vanish in the exterior after the heat replacement (Lemma A.8). The construction has to meet both requirements and still keep the strict stress cone inequalities on the chosen radial intervals (Propositions A.4, A.7 and A.10).

It starts with finite-dimensional moment corrections (Lemmas A.1 and A.2). The same corrections will later attach the axis profile (Proposition B.8) and change the shear (Proposition C.2). Next, the outer profile is built from a given inner reference profile (Section A.2). At the end, its terminal power law EpowE_{\mathrm{pow}} is replaced by an exact heat flow. Compensating moment corrections keep both the pressure datum and the exterior stress conditions unchanged (Lemmas A.6 and A.8 and Proposition A.7).

A.1 Adjusting finitely many moments.

Changing a profile on a compact radial interval changes its cumulative moments in (4.15). Add fixed smooth bumps with adjustable coefficients to correct those changes. The next two results show why this works. Distinct power weights produce independent changes in the moments (Lemma A.1), and the resulting quadratic moment equations can be solved when the discrepancies are small (Lemma A.2). Together with Lemma 4.4, these corrections let each radial change preserve the data already prescribed farther out.

Lemma A.1.

Let α1,…,αm\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m be distinct real numbers. For every jj, let βj\beta_j be a smooth function that is nonnegative, not identically zero, and supported in the interior of a compact interval Ij⊂(0,∞)I_j\subset(0,\infty), where I1<⋯<ImI_1<\cdots<I_m. Then the matrix Bij=∫0∞xαiβj(x)dxB_{ij}=\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha_i}\beta_j(x)\,dx is invertible. The same statement holds in a coordinate obtained by taking a logarithm, where the weights are exponential. If the data vary smoothly over a compact set of parameters and the stated separations remain in place, then the inverse and every fixed parameter derivative of the inverse stay bounded.

Proof.

A nonzero linear combination of mm distinct powers can have at most m−1m-1 distinct positive zeros. To see this, divide by the smallest power. If the quotient had mm zeros, Rolle’s theorem would give m−1m-1 zeros of its derivative. That would contradict the induction hypothesis for the other m−1m-1 powers. It follows that det⁡[xjαi]\det[x_j^{\alpha_i}] is nonzero whenever 0<x1<⋯<xm0<x_1<\cdots<x_m, and its sign stays the same throughout that connected set. Since the determinant is multilinear, det⁡B=∫I1×⋯×Imdet⁡[xjαi]∏jβj(xj)dx1⋯dxm≠0.\det B =\int_{I_1\times\cdots\times I_m}\det[x_j^{\alpha_i}] \prod_j\beta_j(x_j)\,dx_1\cdots dx_m\ne0. The integrand has one sign, and it is nonzero on a set of positive measure. The change of variables x=eyx=e^y proves the logarithmic version. Compactness, together with differentiation of B−1B=IdB^{-1}B=\operatorname{Id}, proves the final statement. That statement does not give a uniform bound for the inverse when two exponents approach each other. ◻

Some moment weights approach each other as λ\lambda tends to zero. The corrections have to stay small enough to preserve the cone, so the proof needs to know how much this costs in the inverse bound. Take identical translated bumps β(y−c1)\beta(y-c_1) and β(y−c2)\beta(y-c_2), and set Δ=c2−c1>0\Delta=c_2-c_1>0 and b(s)=∫estβ(t)dtb(s)=\int e^{st}\beta(t)\,dt. Dividing row ii by esic1e^{s_i c_1} gives B=(b(s1)es1Δb(s1)b(s2)es2Δb(s2)),det⁡B=b(s1)b(s2)(es2Δ−es1Δ).\begin{equation} B= \begin{pmatrix} b(s_1)&e^{s_1\Delta}b(s_1)\\ b(s_2)&e^{s_2\Delta}b(s_2) \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det B=b(s_1)b(s_2)(e^{s_2\Delta}-e^{s_1\Delta}). \tag{A.1} \end{equation}(A.1) Fix the bump and fix Δ>0\Delta>0. Then ‖B−1‖=O(λ−1)\lVert B^{-1}\rVert=O(\lambda^{-1}) when s1−s2=λs_1-s_2=\lambda and the slopes stay in a fixed compact interval. The inverse stays bounded if the limiting separation of the slopes is nonzero. The same O(λ−1)O(\lambda^{-1}) bound holds for moment matrices with weights 1,x−λ1,x^{-\lambda} and bumps on ordered disjoint intervals. This follows by expanding x−λ=1−λlog⁡x+O(λ2)x^{-\lambda}=1-\lambda\log x+O(\lambda^2), because the two bump averages of log⁡x\log x stay strictly separated.

The rank calculation handles the linearized moment map. The actual moments are quadratic in the velocity profiles, so the correction coefficients have to solve a finite system with a quadratic remainder. The next estimate gives a small solution and also controls its parameter derivatives. It does not require all orders of derivatives to be small at the same time.

Lemma A.2.

Let K=[−1,1]K=[-1,1]. Suppose a finite family of correction coefficients c∈ℝmc\in\mathbb{R}^m changes the required moments in the following way. First take the specified linear combinations of the moments, and divide each resulting component by its specified nonzero factor. The change is then Fη(c)=B(η)c+𝒬η(c,c),η∈K.\begin{equation} F_\eta(c)=B(\eta)c+\mathcal Q_\eta(c,c), \qquad \eta\in K. \tag{A.2} \end{equation}(A.2) Here BB and the bilinear map 𝒬\mathcal Q are smooth, BB is invertible on KK, and the given moment discrepancy is d∈C∞(K;ℝm)d\in C^\infty(K;\mathbb{R}^m). Write β0=sup⁡K‖B−1‖\beta_0=\sup_K\lVert B^{-1}\rVert, κ0=sup⁡K‖𝒬‖\kappa_0=\sup_K\lVert\mathcal Q\rVert, and d0=‖d‖C0(K)d_0=\lVert d\rVert_{C^0(K)}. If 8β02κ0d0≤1,8\beta_0^2\kappa_0d_0\le1, there is exactly one solution of Fη(c)=d(η)F_\eta(c)=d(\eta) in the ball ‖c‖C0≤2β0d0\lVert c\rVert_{C^0}\le 2\beta_0d_0. This solution is smooth in η\eta, and iterating c↦B(η)−1(d(η)−𝒬η(c,c))c\mapsto B(\eta)^{-1}(d(\eta)-\mathcal Q_\eta(c,c)) from zero selects it. If 𝒬=0\mathcal Q=0, no smallness condition is needed.

Now choose any finite kk in advance. Let βk\beta_k be the operator norm for multiplication by B−1B^{-1} on Ck(K)C^k(K), and let κk\kappa_k be the corresponding bilinear norm of 𝒬\mathcal Q. Proof.

On .02≤ζb≤9.02\leq\zeta_b\leq 9, the bound goes the other way, R0≥ζb−.02R_0\geq\zeta_b-.02, and integration gives Kb>.20K_b>.20. The main expression in (A.19) is less than −.047-.047 at amplitude .9.9, and greater than .038.038 at amplitude 1.21.2. Its derivative with respect to the amplitude is at least .36.36 throughout that bracket. It follows that, when λ\lambda is small, the full expression has exactly one root in the bracket. The linearization at that root is nonsingular, so it can be inverted locally. This makes the root smooth, and

|∂ηAmp⁡|≤Cpreλ(1+log⁡(1/λ)).\begin{equation} |\partial_\eta\operatorname{Amp}| \leq C_{\mathrm{pre}}\lambda(1+\log(1/\lambda)). \tag{A.20} \end{equation}(A.20) Both equalities in (A.8) now hold. What remains is to check that these moment corrections keep the stress inside its cone. The bounds below prescribe smallness for only finitely many orders of η\eta-derivatives. If smallness bounds are also set for any other finite list of derivative orders, differentiating the integrals and applying Lemma A.2 gives those bounds before the parameters are fixed. Once the parameters have been chosen, every other fixed derivative order still has a finite bound.

A.4 Fixing the pressure datum for the axis profile.

The azimuthal profile EE now fixes the pressure Π0\Pi_0 on the axis by requiring the pressure to vanish at radial infinity, as in (4.25). Proposition B.2 constructs the axis profile analytically. For that construction to work, this pressure datum must extend holomorphically to a neighborhood of [−1,1][-1,1] and must obey the sign and size bounds in Lemma A.5. This subsection checks those facts before the axis is attached. It also shows that the datum does not depend on the later choice of radial scale XRX_R. The pressure integrals here use the global logarithmic coordinate y=log⁡(X/XR)y=\log(X/X_R) on the full reference profile.

Lemma A.5.

Let Eid,schedE_{\mathrm{id,sched}} consist of the reference inner profile (A.7), followed by the outer profile EE from Section A.2. Leave out the azimuthal corrections that preserve the total pressure increment, and leave every other transition interval unchanged. Then the function

Π0(η)=−12∫−∞∞Eid,sched(y,η)2dy\begin{equation} \Pi_0(\eta)=-\frac12\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} E_{\mathrm{id,sched}}(y,\eta)^2\,dy \tag{A.21} \end{equation}(A.21) does not depend on XRX_R and is analytic on a complex neighborhood of [−1,1][-1,1]. It is even. The derivative Π0′(η)\Pi_0'(\eta) has the same sign as η\eta whenever η≠0\eta\neq 0. It also satisfies

Π0(η)≤−52P*2f(η)2.\begin{equation} \Pi_0(\eta)\leq-\frac52P_*^2f(\eta)^2. \tag{A.22} \end{equation}(A.22) For the full reference radial profile, start with this datum and integrate ΠX=E2/(2X)\Pi_X=E^2/(2X). The result is

Π(X,η)=−12∫log⁡(X/XR)∞E(v,η)2dv.\begin{equation} \Pi(X,\eta)=-\frac12\int_{\log(X/X_R)}^\infty E(v,\eta)^2\,dv. \tag{A.23} \end{equation}(A.23)

Proof.

Without the angular bumps, every part of EE can be written as c(y)f(η)ϑ(y)c(y)f(\eta)^{\vartheta(y)}. Here cc and the transition lengths do not depend on η\eta, and 0≤ϑ≤10\leq\vartheta\leq 1. The reference inner profile, the axial transition, the intermediate power-law interval, and the pulse all have ϑ=1\vartheta=1. The profile interpolation lowers this exponent to zero, and the exterior transition and tail have ϑ=0\vartheta=0. The next step is to choose one simply connected neighborhood of the real interval in the complex plane, one connected region in which every closed loop can shrink to a point without leaving the region. Once the poles and zeros are excluded, this property lets one logarithm be chosen consistently throughout the region.

Choose it so that it avoids every pole and zero of ff, and fix an analytic logarithm there, meaning a holomorphic function whose exponential is the original function. Then fϑ=exp⁡(ϑlog⁡f)f^\vartheta=\exp(\vartheta\log f) is holomorphic, with a bound that is uniform for 0≤ϑ≤10\leq\vartheta\leq 1. The squared integrand is bounded by Cey/5Ce^{y/5} as y→−∞y\to-\infty, and by Ce−(1+2h)yCe^{-(1+2h)y} as y→+∞y\to+\infty. The interval between those two tails is finite. Integrating the holomorphic functions with these uniform bounds proves that the pressure datum is analytic.

For real η\eta, differentiating each factor gives ∂ηf2ϑ=−2ϑJ0′f2ϑ\partial_\eta f^{2\vartheta}=-2\vartheta J_0'f^{2\vartheta}. It follows that every term in Π0′\Pi_0' has the same sign as η\eta. The reference inner profile makes the sign strict. That profile contributes exactly −(5/2)P*2f2-(5/2)P_*^2f^2, which proves (A.22). Nothing in the construction in the logarithmic radial coordinate contains XRX_R, so the pressure datum does not depend on that scale. Finally, (A.11) says that putting the angular bumps back changes the total pressure increment by zero. So the full increment is −Π0-\Pi_0, which proves (A.23). ◻

The axis construction can now use this pressure datum. Every later change to the profile must keep the total pressure increment unchanged so that the datum stays fixed. Matching all five radial integrals also keeps the radial velocity and the functions Qs,NsQ_s,N_s unchanged past the correction interval. Suppose an edit has zero total integral of (Enew2−Eold2)/(2X)(E_{\mathrm{new}}^2-E_{\mathrm{old}}^2)/(2X). Then the pressure found by integrating forward is unchanged before and after the edit’s support, although it may change inside that support. A correction to the strict right of XX can be left out of the backward integral (A.23) when it preserves the total pressure increment. Lemma 4.4 gives a stronger result when all five radial moment functions agree at a radius where the two fields meet again. From that radius onward, the radial velocity and the functions Qs,NsQ_s,N_s are restored on the whole later interval, along with their parameter derivatives. The axis construction uses the analytic function Π0\Pi_0, which is already fixed, and integrates pressure forward. Later edits of EE may be smooth without being analytic, but they cannot change that datum. Their total pressure increment is either zero or is restored by the correction that matches all five radial moments. The heat replacement changes the exterior profile while preserving the required convergent differences of moments.

A.6 Replacing the exterior power law with a heat flow.

The reference profile (U,E)(U,E) from Proposition A.4 has the required moments. Past the terminal interval it also has U=0U=0 and E=Epow=c∞X−AE=E_{\mathrm{pow}}=c_\infty X^{-A}. This exterior power law EpowE_{\mathrm{pow}} still leaves a viscous residual. The next step is to replace it outside the annulus with the exact radial swirl heat flow KK from Lemma A.6. After the replacement, the exterior momentum residual is zero, and away from the axis the field has smooth limits at the singular time. The replacement changes three moments. Proposition A.7 restores them with a correction in the second reserved interval ℐ2\mathcal I_2; this also restores the pressure datum Π0\Pi_0 already prescribed for the axis in (A.21).

For a profile that is regular at the axis, let ℛθ(0),ℛz(0)\mathscr R_\theta^{(0)},\mathscr R_z^{(0)} be its leading azimuthal and axial momentum residuals. In the notation of (4.12), this means ℛj(0)=Rj(0)\mathscr R_j^{(0)}=R_j^{(0)}. These residuals include radial viscosity but leave out the higher-order axial viscosity. As in Proposition 4.2, the stress components are Tθ(r)=−r−2∫0rs2ℛθ(0)(s)dsT_\theta(r)=-r^{-2}\int_0^r s^2\mathscr R_\theta^{(0)}(s)\,ds and Tz(r)=−r−1∫0rsℛz(0)(s)dsT_z(r)=-r^{-1}\int_0^r s\mathscr R_z^{(0)}(s)\,ds. The next subsection uses the corrected moment conditions to turn these into integrals from rr to infinity, in Lemma A.8. It then finds the sign and limiting direction of the stress as the outer endpoint is approached, in Proposition A.10.

Write Xb=e3XtailX_b=e^3X_{\mathrm{tail}} and Epow=c∞X−AE_{\mathrm{pow}}=c_\infty X^{-A}, where c∞>0c_\infty>0 does not depend on η\eta. The reference tail is then Epowfo(y)E_{\mathrm{pow}}f_o(y).

ℋ(Z)=1Γ(aK)∫0∞e−vvaK−1(1+Zv)−hdv,Z≥0,\begin{equation} \mathcal H(Z)=\frac1{\Gamma(a_K)}\int_0^\infty e^{-v}v^{a_K-1}(1+Zv)^{-h}\,dv,\qquad Z\geq0, \tag{A.32} \end{equation}(A.32) Here Γ(aK)=∫0∞e−vvaK−1dv\Gamma(a_K)=\int_0^\infty e^{-v}v^{a_K-1}\,dv is the gamma integral, so ℋ(0)=1\mathcal H(0)=1. Lemma A.6.

A.7 Finding the stress from the exterior profile.

This subsection uses the corrected moments for two things. Lemma A.8 shows that the stress is zero outside the annulus, and Proposition A.10 determines the stress direction as the outer edge is approached. First, the moment identities will show that the full weighted integrals of the leading residual are zero. The stress can then be found by integrating from the current radius out to infinity. Once Proposition B.2 and Corollary B.10 have supplied the regular axis and the matching moment conditions, this formula depends only on the exterior profile.

Lemma A.8.

Suppose the leading axisymmetric field is smooth at the axis. Suppose also that it has U=0U=0 and E=Epowfo[1+χK(ℋ(2d/X)−1)]E=E_{\mathrm{pow}}f_o[1+\chi_K(\mathcal H(2d/X)-1)] for y≥0y\geq 0, and that it satisfies the exact moment conditions

Then the leading tangential stresses are zero for X≥XbX\geq X_b. On y≥1/2y\geq 1/2, where χK=1\chi_K=1, equation (A.46) writes them as weighted integrals of the leading residual from rr to infinity, with a positive sign in front of each integral.

The backward integrals contain the cutoff factor, which goes to zero to every order at the outer edge. The next lemma pulls this factor away from a smooth coefficient. This makes it possible to estimate the direction of the stress even as the stress itself goes to zero.

Lemma A.9.

Let c>0c>0, let jj be a fixed nonnegative integer, and let b(u,η)b(u,\eta) be smooth for 0≤u≤δ00\leq u\leq\delta_0 and for η\eta in a compact interval KK. Then there is a coefficient BB such that, whenever 0<δ≤δ00<\delta\leq\delta_0,

Make the substitution u=δ/(1+δ2v)1/2u=\delta/(1+\delta^2v)^{1/2}. Its Jacobian is −12δ3(1+δ2v)−3/2-\tfrac 12\delta^3(1+\delta^2v)^{-3/2}, and c/u2=c/δ2+cvc/u^2=c/\delta^2+cv. This proves (A.47) with

Every fixed mixed derivative of this last integrand is bounded by e−cve^{-cv} times a polynomial in vv, with one bound for the whole closed rectangle of parameters. The stress is zero at the outer edge, so its limiting direction depends on how fast its two components go to zero relative to each other. The backward formula and the flat-integral lemma give both rates. They also give a positive leading coefficient for the angular component.

B Analytic profiles near the axis and how to continue them

This appendix builds the inner part of the leading profile (U,E,Π)(U,E,\Pi). On this inner part, the leading residual stress 𝒯0\mathcal T_0 must be zero, as Proposition B.2 requires. The outer profile has already fixed the pressure datum Π0\Pi_0 on the axis, in Lemma A.5. With that datum fixed, choose the remaining axis data U*,ϕ*U_*,\phi_* and solve the nonlinear profile equations (4.13) on a short radial interval. The solution must be regular at the axis. At its outer endpoint, it must also satisfy the strict shear inequality (B.19), so that Corollary B.10 can continue it toward the outer profile. The large parameter Λ\Lambda in the azimuthal datum (B.3) gives both the analytic solution and the endpoint bounds needed for this continuation, as Propositions B.2 and B.3 show. Equations (4.4)– (4.5) then show that the corresponding velocity is smooth in Cartesian coordinates across the axis.

B.1 Choosing the axis data.

The pressure datum Π0\Pi_0 is already prescribed. The azimuthal datum ϕ*=ϕ(0,η)\phi_*=\phi(0,\eta) and the axial velocity U*U_* on the axis still have to be chosen. Choose them here so that the angular source SqS_q stays positive and the endpoint inequality holds throughout the parameter interval, as Proposition B.3 requires. Equation (B.2) separates the interval into two parts; the azimuthal term gives the needed lower bound on one part, and the axial term gives it on the other.

Use the datum Π0\Pi_0 from Lemma A.5. It is real analytic near [−1,1][-1,1], it is even, and it satisfies

Π0≤−cP*2f2,ηΠ0η>0(η≠0),f=(1+η2)−1.\Pi_0\leq-cP_*^2f^2, \qquad \eta\Pi_{0\eta}>0\quad(\eta\neq 0), \qquad f=(1+\eta^2)^{-1}. Every schedule parameter, including 0<h≤10−20<h\leq 10^{-2}, is already fixed. Choose 0<j0≤.050<j_0\leq .05 small, and set

To see why, note that on (−1,1)(-1,1) the function H*/d=Dη/d+4η+j0H_*/d=D\eta/d+4\eta+j_0 is strictly increasing from −∞-\infty to +∞+\infty. Its zero satisfies |η0|≍j0|\eta_0|\asymp j_0. Also,

−W*=3−8hη2+(1−2h)j0η>2.8,Z*(η0)≥cj0P*2>0.-W_*=3-8h\eta^2+(1-2h)j_0\eta>2.8, \qquad Z_*(\eta_0)\geq cj_0P_*^2>0. B.2 A space for analytic coefficients.

The profile equations (4.13) use parameter derivatives as well as radial derivatives. Their highest radial derivatives are multiplied by the radial variable. At X=0X=0 that multiplier vanishes, so the equations cannot be solved there for their highest radial derivatives in the usual way. The vanishing is only linear, and the smooth power-series coefficients can still be solved one at a time by the radial inverse in (B.5). That is what regular singular point means here. This subsection sets up a weighted coefficient space ℬρ\mathcal B_\rho for the integral form of those equations. Its norm is given in (B.4). In this space, increasing the radial degree makes up for taking a parameter derivative. Lemma B.1 gives the bounds needed for multiplication and radial inversion, the step that solves for a function in the radial variable. Those bounds also cover the mixed nonlinear terms used in the contraction argument for Proposition B.2.

For the analytic construction at the axis, use the scalar radial variable Y=ΛXY=\Lambda X. Fix a small radius ρ>0\rho>0. If F(Y,η)=∑α≥0Fα(η)YαF(Y,\eta)=\sum_{\alpha\geq 0}F_\alpha(\eta)Y^\alpha, define

𝔞αβ=20−αρ−ββ!(α+ββ)(α+1)2(β+1)2,‖F‖ρ=supα,β≥0supη∈I|∂ηβFα(η)|𝔞αβ.\begin{equation} \mathfrak a_{\alpha\beta} =\frac{20^{-\alpha}\rho^{-\beta}\beta!\binom{\alpha+\beta}{\beta}} {(\alpha+1)^2(\beta+1)^2}, \qquad \lVert F\rVert_\rho =\sup_{\alpha,\beta\geq0}\sup_{\eta\in I} \frac{|\partial_\eta^\beta F_\alpha(\eta)|}{\mathfrak a_{\alpha\beta}}. \tag{B.4} \end{equation}(B.4) Let ℬρ\mathcal B_\rho be the set of smooth coefficient sequences whose norm is finite. This space is complete. In a Cauchy sequence, every coefficient and every order of its derivative converges uniformly. Uniform convergence of one derivative after another then shows that these limits are the derivatives of the limiting coefficient. In the rescaled variable YY, the logarithmic radial derivative is 𝒟X=X∂X=Y∂Y\mathcal D_X=X\partial_X=Y\partial_Y. Define ℐF=∫0YF(Y′,η)dY′\mathcal I F=\int_0^Y F(Y',\eta)\,dY'. Rescaling by Y=ΛXY=\Lambda X does not change radial averaging, so 𝒜X(F)=Y−1ℐF\mathcal A_X(F)=Y^{-1}\mathcal I F.

Lemma B.1.

Multiplication is bounded on ℬρ\mathcal B_\rho. For ν=1,2\nu=1,2, let 𝒥νF\mathcal J_\nu F be the solution GG of YGYY+νGY=FYG_{YY}+\nu G_Y=F that extends smoothly to Y=0Y=0 and satisfies G(0)=0G(0)=0. Its coefficients are

(𝒥νF)α+1=Fα(α+1)(α+ν),(𝒥νF)0=0.\begin{equation} (\mathcal J_\nu F)_{\alpha+1} =\frac{F_\alpha}{(\alpha+1)(\alpha+\nu)}, \qquad (\mathcal J_\nu F)_0=0. \tag{B.5} \end{equation}(B.5) The operator 𝒥ν\mathcal J_\nu is bounded on ℬρ\mathcal B_\rho. The same is true of radial averaging, multiplication by YY, and the operators ℐ\mathcal I and ∂ηℐ\partial_\eta\mathcal I. Also,

∥𝒥ν[(∂ηF)(𝒟XG)]∥ρ≤Cρ‖F‖ρ‖G‖ρ.\begin{equation} \bigl\lVert\mathcal J_\nu[(\partial_\eta F)(\mathcal D_XG)]\bigr\rVert_\rho \leq C_\rho\lVert F\rVert_\rho\lVert G\rVert_\rho. \tag{B.6} \end{equation}(B.6) The same estimate still holds if either derivative is left out, or if FF is replaced by 𝒜X(F)\mathcal A_X(F). Extra factors without derivatives may also be inserted, with one more algebra constant for each extra factor.

Proof.

The elementary convolution estimate ∑i=0N(N+1)2(i+1)2(N−i+1)2≤8∑i=1∞i−2=:Csq\begin{equation} \sum_{i=0}^{N}\frac{(N+1)^2}{(i+1)^2(N-i+1)^2} \leq 8\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}i^{-2}=:C_{\mathrm{sq}} \tag{B.7} \end{equation}(B.7) follows by splitting the sum at N/2N/2.

In the Leibniz formula for a product coefficient, the binomial coefficient from differentiation cancels the factorials in the weights. The binomial ratio that remains is at most one, because

80ρ‖F‖ρ‖G‖ρ∑i=0α∑k=0βI1J1N(α+ν)(N+1)2(I1+1)2(J1+1)2(β+1)2(k+1)2(β−k+1)2.\begin{equation*} \frac{80}{\rho}\lVert F\rVert_\rho\lVert G\rVert_\rho \sum_{i=0}^{\alpha}\sum_{k=0}^{\beta} \frac{I_1J_1}{N(\alpha+\nu)} \frac{(N+1)^2}{(I_1+1)^2(J_1+1)^2} \frac{(\beta+1)^2}{(k+1)^2(\beta-k+1)^2}. \end{equation*} Use (B.8) with radial indices I1,J1I_1,J_1 to drop the binomial ratio. This subsection solves the equations (4.13) for the axis data chosen in Section B.1, with the leading residual stress set to zero. Rescale the radius by Y=ΛXY=\Lambda X. B.9 The order of the choices and the completed connection.

This subsection puts all the parameter choices in order and states the completed connection. The matching tolerance in (B.36) depends only on the outer data. Because of these two facts, the amplitude can be chosen to reduce the moment discrepancies before the last transition widths are fixed. The full order is shown in (B.40).

Once the choices are made, derivatives of every other fixed order still have finite bounds, though radial cutoff derivatives may contain inverse powers of the final widths.

Corollary B.10.

The analytic axis profile from Proposition B.2 has a smooth continuation with E>0E>0 for X>0X>0. At log⁡(X/XR)=−5\log(X/X_R)=-5, it matches the reference outer radial profile, including the exact fields, pressure, and radial moment functions. Its leading residual stress is zero through X0X_0. This is followed by an inner collar where the profile remains analytic in η\eta, obeys the admissible stress cone condition, and has the flat factor in (B.30). From there to the matching point, it obeys the strict inequalities of the relaxed cone condition. Its finite parameters can be chosen in the order shown in (B.40).

Proof.

Combine Propositions B.5 and B.8, the fact that p1>2p_1>2 remains true along the profile (B.34), and Corollary B.6. ◻

Corollary B.10 joins the inner and outer profiles E,U,ΠE,U,\Pi with the required pressure datum and radial moments. One condition is still missing on part of the joining interval.

There, the shear (a,−bs)(a,-b_s) obeys only the relaxed cone condition (4.21). The wave construction also needs the inequality vs>2v_s>2 from Lemma 4.5. This appendix makes that inequality hold by changing the shear rapidly in the radial direction, with the change kept away from the axis and the exterior.

The shear is determined by radial derivatives in (4.11), while the cumulative moments 𝔪=(M,I,J,S,Cp)\mathfrak m=(M,I,J,S,C_p) are determined by profile values in (4.15). That difference makes it possible to change the shear by order one while changing the profiles and their moments only a little. First prescribe a periodic family of admissible shears (aL,−bL)(a_L,-b_L) whose mean is the original shear, as in Lemma C.1. Then integrate that family at high radial frequency. A correction on the next reserved interval listed after (A.9) restores all five moments exactly, and this keeps the exterior fields unchanged, as Proposition C.2 proves.

Take the profile supplied by Corollary B.10, Proposition A.4, and Proposition A.7. Proposition B.8 matches the axis profile’s radial moments to the reference outer profile’s moments. That match supplies the regular axis and exact moments required in Lemma A.8. Together, these results fix the input profile E,U,ΠE,U,\Pi used below. This profile and all its parameters stay fixed while the shear is modulated and the moments are corrected in this appendix. Its leading residual stress 𝒯0\mathcal T_0 is nonzero exactly on (Xa,Xb)(X_a,X_b), whose endpoints do not depend on η\eta. The profile obeys the strict inequalities of the relaxed cone condition throughout that interval. It obeys the full admissible stress cone condition on an inner collar and again from the intermediate power-law interval onward, by Propositions A.4, A.7 and A.10. The two edge factorizations are (B.30) and Equations (A.48) to (A.49). Choose a compact interval ℐ=[X−,X+]⋐(Xa,Xb)\mathcal I=[X_-,X_+]\Subset(X_a,X_b) that contains every point where the admissible stress cone condition may fail. It starts inside the first collar where that condition holds and ends in the intermediate power-law interval before its first reserved patch. Shorter collars at XaX_a and XbX_b remain unchanged. Also fix the rectangle near the axis from Corollary B.6, where E/2X,U,V0/X,ΠE/\sqrt{2X},U,V_0/X,\Pi are smooth in X,ηX,\eta and analytic in η\eta on the same complex neighborhood. Choose the rectangle’s radial endpoint inside the shorter inner collar and before X−X_-. Call this endpoint XanX_{\mathrm{an}}.

C.1 A loop with the prescribed mean.

At every profile point, this subsection constructs a family (aL,−bL)(a_L,-b_L) of shear vectors while keeping the integrated residual coefficient psp_s fixed, as stated in Lemma C.1. The family’s average must be (a,−bs)(a,-b_s). Its difference from that original shear then has mean zero, so it has a periodic antiderivative, a periodic function whose derivative is that difference. Proposition C.2 integrates this difference into a small change of the profiles. The family must change smoothly with (X,η)(X,\eta) and must still equal the original shear near the radial boundaries, where nothing needs to change.

Lemma C.1.

Let a,bs,psa,b_s,p_s be smooth on ℐ×[−1,1]\mathcal I\times[-1,1], with a>0a>0, and set ts=−bs/at_s=-b_s/a, vs=a(1+ts2)v_s=a(1+t_s^2). Suppose the strict inequalities of the relaxed cone condition in (4.21) hold everywhere, and suppose the admissible stress cone holds near both radial boundary components. Then there is a smooth loop (aL,−bL)(X,η,φ)(a_L,-b_L)(X,\eta,\varphi), with period one in φ\varphi and aL>0a_L>0, whose mean is the original shear.

∫01(aL,−bL)dφ=(a,−bs).\begin{equation} \int_0^1 (a_L,-b_L)\,d\varphi=(a,-b_s). \tag{C.1} \end{equation}(C.1) Let Ψ\Psi be the vector of cone gaps in (4.35). There are constants κL,δ∂>0\kappa_L,\delta_\partial>0, depending on the fixed data a,bs,ps,ℐa,b_s,p_s,\mathcal I, for which every cone gap has the following uniform lower bound.

Ψj(aL(X,η,φ),bL(X,η,φ),ps(X,η))≥κL,(X,η,φ)∈ℐ×[−1,1]×(ℝ/ℤ),j=1,2,3,4.\begin{equation} \begin{gathered} \Psi_j\bigl(a_L(X,\eta,\varphi),b_L(X,\eta,\varphi),p_s(X,\eta)\bigr)\geq\kappa_L,\\ (X,\eta,\varphi)\in\mathcal I\times[-1,1]\times(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}), \qquad j=1,2,3,4. \end{gathered} \tag{C.2} \end{equation}(C.2) On the radial boundary collars, the loop is exactly the original shear.

(aL,−bL)(X,η,φ)=(a,−bs)(X,η),X∈ℐ,dist⁡(X,∂ℐ)<δ∂,(η,φ)∈[−1,1]×(ℝ/ℤ).\begin{equation} \begin{gathered} (a_L,-b_L)(X,\eta,\varphi)=(a,-b_s)(X,\eta),\\ X\in\mathcal I,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(X,\partial\mathcal I)<\delta_\partial, \qquad (\eta,\varphi)\in[-1,1]\times(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}). \end{gathered} \tag{C.3} \end{equation}(C.3) Every smoothness statement here includes the endpoints of the parameter interval −1≤η≤1-1\leq\eta\leq 1.
